sections.heading: Measurement
paragraphs: Chemistry is built on measured amounts. A measurement has two parts: a number and a unit. The number alone is not enough. Saying "the sample is 5" does not tell you whether that is 5 grams, 5 milliliters, or 5 moles.
A unit is the agreed scale you used. Grams measure mass. Liters measure volume. Seconds measure time. Kelvin measures temperature on the absolute scale used in science.

Scientists use SI units so results can be compared across labs. The SI base units you will meet first are the kilogram (kg) for mass, the meter (m) for length, and the second (s) for time. In chemistry we often use related units that are more handy at the bench: the gram (g), the liter (L), and the milliliter (mL).

Prefixes scale a unit up or down by powers of ten. kilo (k) means 10³, so 1 kg = 1000 g. centi (c) means 10⁻², so 1 cm = 0.01 m. milli (m) means 10⁻³, so 1 mL = 0.001 L. micro (µ) means 10⁻⁶. nano (n) means 10⁻⁹.
Why prefixes exist: writing 0.000001 g is easy to miscount. Writing 1 µg keeps the digit count small and the meaning clear.
sections.why: Every lab number you report must carry a unit. Without the unit, the next student or instrument cannot use your result.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis (unit conversion)
paragraphs: Dimensional analysis is a method for converting one unit into another by multiplying by conversion factors. A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, built from a true equality of units.

Example of a true equality: 1 kg = 1000 g. From that you can write two fractions that both equal 1: (1 kg)/(1000 g) and (1000 g)/(1 kg). You choose the fraction that cancels the unit you want to remove.

Units cancel the same way numbers cancel in a fraction. If grams appear on top and bottom, those grams cancel. What remains is the unit you want. That is why the method is reliable: a wrong conversion factor leaves the wrong unit in the answer, so you can catch the mistake before you finish.

worked.title: Convert 2.50 kg to grams
steps: Write what you start with, including the unit: 2.50 kg.
Write the equality that links kg and g: 1 kg = 1000 g.
Build the conversion factor that puts kg on the bottom so kg will cancel: (1000 g)/(1 kg).
Multiply: 2.50 kg × (1000 g)/(1 kg).
Cancel the kg unit on top with the kg unit on the bottom.
Compute the number: 2.50 × 1000 = 2500.
The remaining unit is g. So the exact product is 2500 g.
Check significant figures. 2.50 has 3 significant figures. 1000 in this equality is an exact defined count (kilo means exactly 1000), so it does not limit sig figs.
Report 2.50 × 10³ g, or 2500 g with a clear note that 3 sig figs apply. Prefer scientific notation when trailing zeros would be unclear: 2.50 × 10³ g.

workedExamples.title: Convert 375 mL to liters
steps: Start with 375 mL.
Equality: 1 L = 1000 mL.
Choose the factor with mL on the bottom: (1 L)/(1000 mL).
Cancel mL.
Unit left: L. Result so far: 0.375 L.
Sig figs: 375 has 3 significant figures (leading zeros after a decimal would not count, but here the digits are 3, 7, 5). The 1000 mL per L is exact.
Final answer: 0.375 L.

sections.heading: Significant figures
paragraphs: Significant figures (sig figs) are the digits in a measured value that are known with confidence, plus one estimated digit. They tell the reader how precise the measurement was.
Why they matter: if a balance only reads to 0.01 g, writing 12.3444 g pretends you know more than the instrument can show. Sig figs stop you from inventing precision.
Counting rules for a written number:
1. Non-zero digits (1 to 9) are always significant. Example: 23.4 has 3 sig figs.
2. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Example: 1002 has 4 sig figs.
3. Leading zeros (zeros before the first non-zero digit) are not significant. They only place the decimal. Example: 0.00456 has 3 sig figs (4, 5, 6).
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. Example: 12.30 has 4 sig figs. The final zero means the tenths place was measured as zero, not left blank.

5. Trailing zeros in a whole number with no decimal point are ambiguous. 1500 might have 2, 3, or 4 sig figs. Avoid the ambiguity by writing scientific notation: 1.5 × 10³ (2 sig figs) or 1.500 × 10³ (4 sig figs).

worked.title: How many sig figs in 0.02050?
steps: Write the number: 0.02050.
Leading zeros before 2 are not significant. Drop 0.0 from the count.
Digits that remain in view: 2, 0, 5, 0.
The zero between 2 and 5 is between non-zero digits, so it counts.
The trailing zero after the decimal (the last 0) counts because it sits after the decimal point.
Total: 4 significant figures (2, 0, 5, 0).

sections.heading: Sig figs when you calculate
paragraphs: Multiplication and division use one rule. Addition and subtraction use a different rule. Mixing the two rules is a common source of wrong answers.

Multiplication and division: the result may have only as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures. Why: each measured factor contributes uncertainty, and the weakest link sets the limit.

Addition and subtraction: look at decimal places, not at the count of sig figs. The result may have only as many digits after the decimal as the addend with the fewest digits after the decimal. Why: you cannot know a hundredths place if one of the numbers only went to tenths.

worked.title: Multiply 4.56 g × 1.4 (density-style product)
steps: Identify the operation: multiplication.
Count sig figs in 4.56: 3 sig figs.
Count sig figs in 1.4: 2 sig figs.
The tighter limit is 2 sig figs.
Compute the raw product: 4.56 × 1.4 = 6.384.
Round 6.384 to 2 sig figs. Look at the first two digits: 6 and 3. The next digit is 8, which is 5 or greater, so round the 3 up to 4.
Final answer: 6.4 (with the product's unit).

workedExamples.title: Add 12.11 mL + 0.3 mL + 1.007 mL
steps: Identify the operation: addition.
Look at decimal places, not total sig figs.
12.11 has 2 digits after the decimal.
0.3 has 1 digit after the decimal.
1.007 has 3 digits after the decimal.
The strictest limit is 1 digit after the decimal (from 0.3).
Round 13.417 so only 1 digit remains after the decimal. The tenths digit is 4. The next digit is 1, which is less than 5, so the 4 stays.
Final answer: 13.4 mL.

mistake.wrong: Treating 12.00 g + 1.1 g like a multiplication problem and cutting the answer to 2 sig figs as 13 g.
mistake.whyWrong: Addition is limited by decimal places, not by the sig-fig count. 12.00 is known to the hundredths place. 1.1 is known only to the tenths place. The sum must stop at tenths, which gives 13.1 g, not a 2-sig-fig chop to 13 g.
mistake.correct: 12.00 + 1.1 = 13.10 raw, then round to one digit after the decimal because of 1.1. Answer: 13.1 g.

sections.heading: Density
paragraphs: Density is mass per unit volume. As a formula: density ρ = m / V. If mass is in grams and volume is in milliliters, density has units g/mL. For solids you will also see g/cm³. 1 mL = 1 cm³ by definition, so g/mL and g/cm³ match for this purpose.

Why density is useful: it lets you convert between mass and volume for a pure substance when you know one of them. Water near room temperature has a density of about 1.00 g/mL. That is a standard value you may use unless a problem gives a different temperature value.
Rearrangements you will need: m = ρ × V, and V = m / ρ. Always write the units in the setup so they cancel to the unit you want.

worked.title: Mass of 25.0 mL of a liquid with density 0.789 g/mL
steps: Write the given volume: V = 25.0 mL.
Write the given density: ρ = 0.789 g/mL.
Choose the form that solves for mass: m = ρ × V.
Substitute with units: m = 0.789 g/mL × 25.0 mL.
Cancel mL on top and bottom.
Multiply the numbers: 0.789 × 25.0.
0.789 × 25 = 19.725; keep the extra place for now: 19.725.
Sig figs for multiplication: 0.789 has 3 sig figs; 25.0 has 3 sig figs. Limit = 3 sig figs.
Round 19.725 to 3 sig figs. Digits: 1, 9, 7. Next digit is 2, so do not round up.
Final answer: 19.7 g.

workedExamples.title: Volume of 40.0 g of a metal with density 8.96 g/cm³
steps: Given: m = 40.0 g; ρ = 8.96 g/cm³.
Solve for volume: V = m / ρ.
Set up: V = 40.0 g / (8.96 g/cm³).
Cancel g.
Sig figs: 40.0 has 3; 8.96 has 3. Limit = 3 sig figs.
Round 4.464... to 3 sig figs: 4.46.
Final answer: 4.46 cm³.

sections.heading: The nuclear atom
paragraphs: An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus and a much larger cloud of electrons around it. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons. Protons have a charge of +1. Electrons have a charge of −1. Neutrons have charge 0.
The atomic number Z is the number of protons. Z defines the element. Every carbon atom has Z = 6. Every iron atom has Z = 26.
The mass number A is the total number of protons plus neutrons in that nucleus. Neutrons = A − Z. Electrons are not part of A because their mass is tiny compared with protons and neutrons.
In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. That keeps the total charge at zero.

A helpful picture: if the nucleus were the size of a marble, the electron cloud would stretch across a sports stadium. Almost all of an atom's mass sits in that tiny nucleus. Almost all of its volume is the electron cloud.
Chemists write a nuclide as ᴬX or as X-A. The element symbol already encodes Z, so you do not need to write Z unless you want the full form ᴬ<sub>Z</sub>X.
sections.why: Z and A are the two labels you need before you can count particles in any atom or ion. Without them, the rest of the chapter has nothing to stand on.

figure.alt: Diagram of an iron-56 Fe3+ ion: nucleus with 26 protons and 30 neutrons, and an electron cloud with 23 electrons after losing three.

sections.heading: Isotopes and ions
paragraphs: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A). Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons.
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a net charge. A cation has lost electrons and is positive. An anion has gained electrons and is negative.
For a monoatomic ion, charge = protons − electrons. Rearranged: electrons = protons − charge. For Fe³⁺, Z = 26 and charge = +3, so electrons = 26 − 3 = 23.
Isotope symbols you will see often: ¹H (protium), ²H or D (deuterium), ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C, ²³⁵U, ²³⁸U. Same Z within each element; different A.
When a problem says "an atom of iron-56," it means A = 56 and Z = 26. When it says "the Fe³⁺ ion," you still use Z = 26 for protons, then adjust electrons for the charge.

worked.title: Particles in ⁵⁶Fe³⁺
steps: Read the nuclide symbol. The mass number A is the upper left number: 56. The element is Fe, so look up Z for iron: Z = 26.
Protons = Z = 26.
Neutrons = A − Z = 56 − 26 = 30.
The ion charge is 3+, written as Fe³⁺. That means the ion has three fewer electrons than protons.
Electrons = protons − charge = 26 − 3 = 23.
Summary: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons.

workedExamples.title: Particles in ³⁵Cl⁻
steps: A = 35. Element Cl has Z = 17.
Protons = 17.
Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.
Charge is 1−, so the ion has one extra electron compared with the neutral atom.
Electrons = protons − (charge) = 17 − (−1) = 18.
Summary: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons.

sections.heading: Average atomic mass
paragraphs: Most elements in nature are mixtures of isotopes. The atomic mass on the periodic table is not the mass of one isotope. It is a weighted average of the isotope masses, weighted by how common each isotope is.

Formula: average atomic mass = Σ (fractional abundance × isotopic mass). Fractional abundance is the percent abundance divided by 100. The sum of all fractional abundances for an element must equal 1.
Isotopic masses are measured on a mass spectrometer and are close to, but not exactly equal to, the integer mass numbers. Use the given isotopic mass in u (unified atomic mass units), not A itself.
The unit u (also written amu in older texts) is defined so that a ¹²C atom has mass exactly 12 u. Other isotope masses are measured relative to that standard.
If a problem gives only two isotopes, you need both abundances and both masses. If it gives one abundance, the other is 100% minus that value, but only when exactly two isotopes are present.

worked.title: Average atomic mass of chlorine
steps: Data (standard textbook values): ³⁵Cl is 75.77% abundant with mass 34.969 u. ³⁷Cl is 24.23% abundant with mass 36.966 u.
Convert percents to fractions: 75.77% → 0.7577. 24.23% → 0.2423.
Check that the fractions add to 1: 0.7577 + 0.2423 = 1.0000. Good.
Contribution from ³⁵Cl: 0.7577 × 34.969 = 26.4960... u. Keep extra digits for now.
Contribution from ³⁷Cl: 0.2423 × 36.966 = 8.9569... u.
Add the contributions: 26.4960 + 8.9569 = 35.4529... u.
Round to match the usual table precision (two decimals for Cl): 35.45 u.
Final answer: 35.45 u. That matches the periodic-table value for chlorine.

workedExamples.title: Average atomic mass of bromine
steps: Data: ⁷⁹Br is 50.69% with mass 78.918 u. ⁸¹Br is 49.31% with mass 80.916 u.
Fractions: 0.5069 and 0.4931. Sum = 1.0000.
Round to two decimals as on many tables: 79.90 u.
Final answer: 79.90 u.

mistake.wrong: Averaging the two chlorine isotope masses as (34.969 + 36.966)/2 = 35.968 u and calling that the atomic mass.
mistake.whyWrong: A simple mean treats both isotopes as equally common. Chlorine is not 50/50. ³⁵Cl is about three times as common as ³⁷Cl, so the average must sit closer to 35 than to 37.
mistake.correct: Weight each mass by its fractional abundance, then add. For Cl that gives about 35.45 u, not 35.97 u.

sections.heading: The mole and Avogadro's number
paragraphs: The mole (symbol mol) is the SI unit for amount of substance. One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles. Avogadro's number N<sub>A</sub> = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. The particles may be atoms, molecules, ions, or formula units, depending on what you are counting.
Molar mass M is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol. Numerically, the molar mass in g/mol equals the formula mass in u. Water has formula mass 18.02 u, so M(H₂O) = 18.02 g/mol.

Why that match works: by definition, 1 u is tied to 1/12 the mass of a ¹²C atom, and the mole is defined so that 12 g of ¹²C is exactly 1 mol. The same scale links u and g/mol for every other substance.
Saying "1 mol of water" means 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules. Saying "1 mol of NaCl" means 6.022 × 10²³ formula units of NaCl.
Standard atomic molar masses used here (g/mol): H = 1.008, C = 12.01, N = 14.01, O = 16.00, Na = 22.99, Cl = 35.45, Fe = 55.85. Use a problem's given value if it differs slightly.
sections.why: Lab balances read grams. Reaction equations talk in moles. The mole is the bridge between the two languages.

sections.heading: Mass, moles, and particles
paragraphs: Three linked conversions cover almost every early mole problem:
1. Mass ↔ moles: n = m / M, and m = n × M. Mass m is in grams. Molar mass M is in g/mol. Amount n is in mol.
2. Moles ↔ particles: N = n × N<sub>A</sub>, and n = N / N<sub>A</sub>. N is a count of particles (no unit, or sometimes written as molecules or atoms).
3. Never multiply grams directly by N<sub>A</sub>. That skips the mole step and gives a meaningless number. Always go grams → moles → particles, or the reverse.

Dimensional analysis still applies. Write every unit in the setup. Grams cancel when you multiply by (1 mol)/(M g). Moles cancel when you multiply by N<sub>A</sub>. If the leftover unit is wrong, the conversion factor was upside down.

For compounds, "particles" usually means molecules. For ionic solids, "particles" usually means formula units. For elements that form diatomic molecules (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂), be clear whether the problem asks for moles of molecules or moles of atoms.

worked.title: Moles of water in 10.0 g H₂O
steps: Write the formula mass of H₂O from atomic molar masses: H = 1.008 g/mol, O = 16.00 g/mol.
M(H₂O) = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 2.016 + 16.00 = 18.016 g/mol. Round to 18.02 g/mol for three-to-four significant use (standard table style).
Given mass m = 10.0 g.
Use n = m / M.
Set up: n = 10.0 g / (18.02 g/mol).
Cancel g.
Sig figs: 10.0 has 3 sig figs. 18.02 has 4. Limit = 3 sig figs.
Round 0.5549... to 3 sig figs: 0.555.
Final answer: 0.555 mol H₂O.

workedExamples.title: How many molecules in 0.555 mol H₂O?
steps: Start with n = 0.555 mol H₂O (from the previous example).
Use N = n × N<sub>A</sub> with N<sub>A</sub> = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Set up: N = 0.555 mol × (6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol).
Cancel mol.
Sig figs: 0.555 has 3; 6.022 has 4. Limit = 3 sig figs.
Final answer: 3.34 × 10²³ molecules of H₂O.

workedExamples.title: Mass of 2.50 × 10²² atoms of Fe
steps: Convert particles to moles first: n = N / N<sub>A</sub>.
n = (2.50 × 10²² atoms) / (6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol).
Divide the powers of ten: 10²² / 10²³ = 10⁻¹. Numbers: 2.50 / 6.022 = 0.4151...
n = 0.4151... × 10⁻¹ = 0.04151... mol Fe. Keep extra digits.
Molar mass of Fe from the table: 55.85 g/mol.
Sig figs: 2.50 × 10²² has 3 sig figs. Round mass to 3 sig figs.
Final answer: 2.32 g Fe.

sections.heading: Empirical and molecular formulas
paragraphs: A chemical formula tells which elements are present and in what ratio. An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom in one molecule. The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
Example: hydrogen peroxide has molecular formula H₂O₂. The simplest ratio is HO, so the empirical formula is HO. Glucose has molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and empirical formula CH₂O.

Ionic compounds are usually written as empirical formulas (the formula unit), because a crystal does not contain separate neutral molecules of NaCl. Molecular compounds can have empirical and molecular formulas that differ.
Subscripts in a formula are fixed by nature for that compound. You may not change them to balance an equation; you change coefficients in front of formulas instead.
Hydrates such as CuSO₄·5H₂O count the water molecules in the formula mass. M(CuSO₄·5H₂O) = M(CuSO₄) + 5×M(H₂O).
Structural formulas and condensed structural formulas show connectivity (for example CH₃COOH for acetic acid). Those are richer than the molecular formula C₂H₄O₂, which only gives atom counts.
sections.why: Lab analysis often gives the empirical formula first. You need a molar mass from another experiment before you can lift that ratio up to the true molecular formula.

sections.heading: Mass percent composition
paragraphs: Mass percent of an element in a compound = (mass of that element in 1 mol of compound / molar mass of the compound) × 100%.

Build the molar mass from atomic molar masses. Count every atom in the formula. If an element appears in two places (as in NH₄NO₃, which has N in both the ammonium and the nitrate parts), add both contributions.
Mass percents of all elements in a compound must add to 100% (within rounding). That is a quick check after you finish.
Percent composition does not tell you how atoms are connected. CH₂O could be formaldehyde, acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂ has the same empirical formula), or glucose. Connectivity needs more information.

Worked percent problems almost always ask for one element, but you can compute all elements the same way. If three elements' percents add to about 100%, your molar mass and atom counts are consistent.

worked.title: Mass percent of N in NH₄NO₃
steps: Write atomic molar masses: N = 14.01, H = 1.008, O = 16.00 g/mol.
Mass of N in 1 mol of NH₄NO₃: there are 2 N atoms, so 2 × 14.01 = 28.02 g.
Sig figs: inputs support 4 figures in the masses; percent is commonly reported to 3 significant figures here as 35.0%, or to one decimal as 35.0%.
Final answer: 35.0% N.

workedExamples.title: Mass percent of O in CO₂
steps: Mass of O in 1 mol = 32.00 g.
Round to four significant figures matching the inputs: 72.71% O.
Final answer: 72.71% O.

sections.heading: Empirical formula from percent composition
paragraphs: A standard path turns percent composition into an empirical formula:
1. Assume you have 100.0 g of the compound. Then each percent becomes a mass in grams.
2. Convert each element's mass to moles using its molar mass.
3. Divide every mole amount by the smallest mole amount. That gives a ratio near whole numbers.
4. If you get values like 1.50 or 1.33, multiply all ratio numbers by 2 or 3 to clear the fraction. Then write the subscripts.
Rounding tip: ratios like 1.98 or 2.02 are almost certainly 2. Ratios like 1.25 suggest multiply by 4 (1.25 × 4 = 5). Ratios like 1.33 suggest multiply by 3 (1.33 × 3 = 4).
If the analysis data come as masses instead of percents, skip the "assume 100 g" step and convert the given masses to moles directly.

Significant figures in empirical-formula work: mole amounts may look messy (3.3306…), but the final ratio should clean up to whole numbers within about 0.1. If it does not, recheck the arithmetic or the given percents.

worked.title: 40.0% C, 6.71% H, 53.3% O → empirical formula
steps: Assume 100.0 g of sample. Then masses are 40.0 g C, 6.71 g H, 53.3 g O.
Moles of C: 40.0 g / 12.01 g/mol = 3.3306... mol C.
Moles of H: 6.71 g / 1.008 g/mol = 6.6567... mol H.
Moles of O: 53.3 g / 16.00 g/mol = 3.33125 mol O.
Smallest mole amount ≈ 3.331 mol (C and O are equal).
Whole-number ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1.
Empirical formula: CH₂O.

mistake.wrong: Treating the percent numbers as already being moles and writing C₄₀H₇O₅₃.
mistake.whyWrong: Percent is a mass fraction, not a mole count. Carbon atoms and oxygen atoms have different masses, so 40 g of C is not the same number of moles as 40 g of O.
mistake.correct: Convert each percent-as-grams into moles first, then divide by the smallest mole amount to get the atom ratio.

sections.heading: Molecular formula from empirical formula
paragraphs: Once you have the empirical formula, you still need the molar mass of the real compound (from osmometry, mass spectrometry, or the problem statement).
Compute the empirical-formula mass (the mass of one empirical unit). Then n = (molar mass) / (empirical-formula mass). Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by that whole number n.
If n comes out to 1.00, the empirical and molecular formulas are the same. That is common for many ionic compounds and for some small molecules like H₂O and CH₄.
Always recompute the molar mass from your final molecular formula and check that it matches the given molar mass within rounding.

worked.title: CH₂O with molar mass 180. g/mol
steps: Empirical formula: CH₂O.
Empirical-formula mass = 12.01 + 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 12.01 + 2.016 + 16.00 = 30.026 g per empirical unit. Use 30.03 g/mol.
Given molar mass of the compound = 180. g/mol (3 sig figs; the trailing decimal marks the zero as significant).
n must be a whole number. Round 5.994 to 6.
Multiply subscripts by 6: C₆H₁₂O₆.
Final answer: molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).

workedExamples.title: Empirical HO with molar mass 34.02 g/mol
steps: Empirical-formula mass of HO = 1.008 + 16.00 = 17.008 g/mol.
Multiply: H₂O₂.
Final answer: H₂O₂.

sections.heading: Oxidation states
paragraphs: An oxidation state (oxidation number) is a bookkeeping charge assigned to an atom in a compound. It is not always the real charge on that atom. It is a tool for tracking electron transfer in redox chemistry.
Standard rules, applied in order:
1. An atom in its elemental form has oxidation state 0 (examples: Fe(s), O₂, H₂, S₈).
2. A monoatomic ion has oxidation state equal to its charge (Na⁺ is +1, Cl⁻ is −1, Fe³⁺ is +3).
3. Fluorine in compounds is always −1.
4. Hydrogen is +1 when bonded to nonmetals, and −1 in metal hydrides (NaH).
5. Oxygen is usually −2. Exceptions: peroxides (H₂O₂) where O is −1, and OF₂ where O is +2.
6. The sum of oxidation states in a neutral molecule is 0. In a polyatomic ion, the sum equals the ion charge.

Group trend shortcuts that match the rules: alkali metals (Group 1) in compounds are +1. Alkaline earth metals (Group 2) are +2. Halogens are usually −1 when they are the most electronegative atom in the compound.

Oxidation states can be fractional in averages for some compounds (for example, Fe₃O₄), but intro problems almost always give integer states. Stick to the integer rules above unless a problem says otherwise.

In redox later, oxidation means an increase in oxidation state (electron loss in the bookkeeping sense). Reduction means a decrease in oxidation state. Assigning states correctly is the first step in identifying what was oxidized and what was reduced.

Peroxide check: in H₂O₂ each oxygen is −1, not −2. If you blindly assign O = −2 in H₂O₂, hydrogen would have to be +2 to keep the molecule neutral, which breaks the hydrogen rule. Spot the O–O single bond and switch to the peroxide exception.

worked.title: Oxidation state of N in NO₃⁻
steps: The ion charge is −1, so the sum of oxidation states = −1.
There are 3 oxygen atoms. Each O is −2 (not a peroxide or OF₂ case).
Total from oxygen: 3 × (−2) = −6.
Let the oxidation state of N be x.
Final answer: N is +5 in NO₃⁻.

workedExamples.title: Oxidation state of C in CO₂ and of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻
steps: CO₂ is neutral, so the sum is 0. Two O at −2 each give −4. Let C be x: x − 4 = 0 → x = +4. Carbon is +4.
Cr₂O₇²⁻ has charge −2. Seven O at −2 each give −14. Let each Cr be y. Two Cr give 2y.
y = 6. Each Cr is +6.

sections.heading: Chemical equations and why we balance them
paragraphs: A chemical equation is a compact sentence that shows reactants turning into products. Reactants are written on the left. Products are written on the right. An arrow points from reactants to products.
Example skeleton: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. This is not yet ready to use for amounts, because it is not balanced.

Balanced means each element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Why we balance: atoms are not created or destroyed in ordinary chemical change (conservation of mass). A balanced equation is the bookkeeping that respects that rule.

Coefficients are the numbers placed in front of formulas. They scale the whole formula. In 2 H₂O the coefficient 2 means two water molecules (or two moles of water). Subscripts inside a formula are part of the identity of the substance. You may change coefficients when balancing. You must not change subscripts, or you invent a different compound.
States of matter in parentheses are optional helpers: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. They do not change the atom count.

worked.title: Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
steps: Count atoms on the left: H = 2, O = 2.
Count atoms on the right: H = 2, O = 1.
Oxygen is short on the right. Place coefficient 2 in front of H₂O: H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Recount the right side: H = 4, O = 2.
Hydrogen on the left is now short (only 2). Place coefficient 2 in front of H₂: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Recount left: H = 4, O = 2. Right: H = 4, O = 2.
Both sides match. The balanced equation is 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Read it in moles when you do stoichiometry: 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ to make 2 mol H₂O.

sections.why: A balanced equation gives the mole ratios you need for every later stoichiometry step. An unbalanced equation gives false ratios.

sections.heading: Mole ratios from the balanced equation
paragraphs: The mole (mol) is the chemist's counting unit for particles. One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). For stoichiometry you mostly need this idea: a balanced equation's coefficients are mole ratios.
From 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O you may write ratios such as (2 mol H₂)/(1 mol O₂) or (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂). Each of those fractions equals 1 in the sense of a conversion factor between the linked amounts.

Molar mass converts grams to moles and moles to grams. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in g/mol. You build it from atomic molar masses on the periodic table. Standard values we use here: H = 1.008 g/mol, C = 12.01 g/mol, O = 16.00 g/mol, N = 14.01 g/mol, Na = 22.99 g/mol, Cl = 35.45 g/mol.

worked.title: Simple: moles of water from 3.00 mol H₂ (excess O₂)
steps: Balanced equation: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Given: 3.00 mol H₂. Oxygen is in excess, so H₂ limits the product.
Write the mole ratio that links H₂ to H₂O from the coefficients: (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
That ratio simplifies to (1 mol H₂O)/(1 mol H₂), but keep it clear: multiply by (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Set up: 3.00 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Cancel mol H₂.
Unit left: mol H₂O.
Sig figs: 3.00 has 3 sig figs. Coefficients are exact. Answer: 3.00 mol H₂O.

sections.heading: Grams to grams through moles
paragraphs: Lab balances read grams, not moles. So a full stoichiometry path is usually: grams of A → moles of A → moles of B → grams of B. The middle step uses the mole ratio from the balanced equation. The outer steps use molar masses.
Never multiply grams of A by a mole ratio as if grams were moles. That skips the conversion and gives a wrong size answer.

worked.title: Harder: mass of H₂O from 10.0 g H₂ with excess O₂
steps: Balanced equation: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Given mass: 10.0 g H₂. O₂ is excess.
Molar mass of H₂: 2 × 1.008 = 2.016 g/mol.
Convert grams H₂ to moles H₂: 10.0 g H₂ × (1 mol H₂)/(2.016 g H₂).
Cancel g H₂.
Compute moles H₂: 10.0 / 2.016 = 4.960317... mol H₂. Keep extra digits for now: 4.960317 mol H₂.
Apply the mole ratio to water: 4.960317 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Cancel mol H₂. Moles H₂O = 4.960317 mol H₂O.
Convert to grams: 4.960317 mol H₂O × (18.016 g H₂O)/(1 mol H₂O).
Cancel mol H₂O.
Sig figs: the given 10.0 g has 3 sig figs. Atomic masses used here are treated as at least as precise. Round the final mass to 3 sig figs.
89.365... rounds to 89.4 g because the digit after 3 is 6.
Final answer: 89.4 g H₂O.

sections.heading: Limiting reactant and percent yield
paragraphs: When two reactants are both given in limited amounts, one will run out first. That reactant is the limiting reactant (limiting reagent). It caps how much product can form. The other reactant is in excess. Some of it will be left over.

How to find the limiting reactant: convert each given amount to moles of product using the mole ratios. The reactant that produces the smaller amount of product is limiting. Use only that smaller amount for later yield calculations.
Theoretical yield is the mass of product predicted by stoichiometry from the limiting reactant, assuming the reaction goes to completion with no losses.
Actual yield is the mass you obtain in the lab. It is almost always less than theoretical yield because of incomplete reaction, side reactions, or loss during transfer.
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%. Both yields must use the same unit, usually grams.

worked.title: Limiting reactant: 5.00 g H₂ and 40.0 g O₂ making water
steps: Balanced equation: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Moles of H₂: 5.00 g × (1 mol / 2.016 g) = 2.48016 mol H₂.
Moles of O₂: molar mass O₂ = 32.00 g/mol. 40.0 g × (1 mol / 32.00 g) = 1.250 mol O₂.
Moles of H₂O from H₂ if H₂ is fully used: 2.48016 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂) = 2.48016 mol H₂O.
Moles of H₂O from O₂ if O₂ is fully used: 1.250 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(1 mol O₂) = 2.500 mol H₂O.
Compare 2.48016 mol and 2.500 mol. The smaller is 2.48016 mol. So H₂ is limiting.
Theoretical moles of water = 2.48016 mol.
Theoretical mass: 2.48016 mol × 18.016 g/mol = 44.682... g.
Round to 3 sig figs to match 5.00 g: 44.7 g H₂O theoretical.

workedExamples.title: Percent yield if the lab collects 40.0 g H₂O from the run above
steps: Actual yield = 40.0 g.
Theoretical yield from the previous example = 44.7 g.
Percent yield = (40.0 / 44.7) × 100%.
Sig figs: 40.0 and 44.7 each have 3 sig figs. Report 3 sig figs in the percentage.
Final answer: 89.5% yield.

mistake.wrong: Picking the limiting reactant as whichever reactant has the smaller mass in grams (here choosing H₂ only because 5.00 g < 40.0 g) without converting to moles of product.
mistake.whyWrong: Grams of different substances are not comparable as amounts of reaction. O₂ molecules are heavier than H₂ molecules. You must compare how much product each given amount can make, using moles and the balanced coefficients.
mistake.correct: Convert each reactant to moles of product. The smaller product amount wins. In the example, H₂ still was limiting, but that conclusion came from 2.48 mol H₂O vs 2.50 mol H₂O, not from comparing 5 g to 40 g.

sections.heading: Solution dilution
paragraphs: Concentration in many early problems is molarity. Molarity M = moles of solute / liters of solution. A 0.50 M NaCl solution has 0.50 mol NaCl in each 1.00 L of solution.

Dilution means adding solvent (usually water) to a concentrated stock solution. The number of moles of solute stays the same. Only the volume changes. That is why the dilution equation works: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. The product M×V is proportional to moles when volume is in liters (or when both volumes use the same unit).
M₁ and V₁ are the molarity and volume of the stock piece you measure out. M₂ and V₂ are the molarity and volume of the diluted solution after you add solvent and mix.

worked.title: Prepare 250. mL of 0.100 M HCl from 1.00 M HCl stock
steps: Identify: M₁ = 1.00 M (stock), M₂ = 0.100 M (diluted), V₂ = 250. mL.
Keep volume units consistent. Convert V₂ to liters: 250. mL × (1 L)/(1000 mL) = 0.250 L.
Write M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ and solve for V₁: V₁ = (M₂V₂)/M₁.
Substitute: V₁ = (0.100 mol/L × 0.250 L) / (1.00 mol/L).
Compute the numerator: 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol (the moles of HCl needed).
Divide by M₁: 0.0250 mol / 1.00 mol/L = 0.0250 L.
Convert V₁ to mL if that is how you will pipette: 0.0250 L × 1000 mL/L = 25.0 mL.
Sig figs: 0.100, 250., and 1.00 each support 3 sig figs. Answer: measure 25.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl and add water until the total volume is 250. mL.

items.a: 6.0 mol H₂ × (2 mol NH₃)/(3 mol H₂) = 4.0 mol NH₃.

You need 500. mL of 0.200 M NaCl from 1.00 M stock. What volume of stock do you take?
items.a: V₁ = (0.200 × 0.500 L)/1.00 = 0.100 L = 100. mL of stock, then dilute to 500. mL.

sections.heading: Light as energy packets
paragraphs: Visible light is one slice of electromagnetic radiation. Every wave has a wavelength λ (distance from crest to crest) and a frequency ν (number of oscillations per second). They are linked by c = λν, where c is the speed of light in vacuum, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s.

Planck and Einstein showed that light also comes in packets called photons. The energy of one photon is E = hν, where h is Planck's constant, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Combining with c = λν gives E = hc / λ.
Units to watch: λ must be in meters when you use c in m/s. A wavelength given in nm must be converted: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.
Frequency has SI unit s⁻¹, also called hertz (Hz). Wavelength for visible light is often quoted in nm: violet near 400 nm, red near 700 nm. Shorter λ means higher ν and higher E per photon.
A mole of photons has energy N<sub>A</sub> × E<sub>photon</sub>. That quantity is useful when you compare photon energy to chemical bond energies given per mole.

Infrared photons have longer wavelength and lower energy than visible photons. Ultraviolet photons have shorter wavelength and higher energy. That is why UV light can break bonds that visible light leaves alone.
sections.why: Spectroscopy, Bohr jumps, and every later quantum formula start from E = hν. If λ and ν are swapped or units are wrong, the energy is wrong by orders of magnitude.

worked.title: Energy of a 486.1 nm photon (Balmer H-β)
steps: Write λ = 486.1 nm.
Convert to meters: 486.1 nm × (10⁻⁹ m)/(1 nm) = 4.861 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Write E = hc / λ with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s.
First compute hc: (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(2.998 × 10⁸) = 1.986 × 10⁻²⁵ J·m (to four figures).
Cancel m. Divide the numbers: 1.986 / 4.861 = 0.4086. Powers of ten: 10⁻²⁵ / 10⁻⁷ = 10⁻¹⁸.
Sig figs: 486.1 has 4 sig figs. Report E = 4.086 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Final answer: 4.086 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon.

workedExamples.title: Frequency of the same 486.1 nm light
steps: Use ν = c / λ.
λ = 4.861 × 10⁻⁷ m (from above).
Final answer: 6.167 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

workedExamples.title: Energy of 1.00 mol of 486.1 nm photons
steps: From earlier, one 486.1 nm photon has E = 4.086 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
For 1.00 mol of photons, multiply by N<sub>A</sub> = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
E<sub>molar</sub> = (4.086 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) × (6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).
Multiply numbers: 4.086 × 6.022 = 24.61. Powers: 10⁻¹⁹ × 10²³ = 10⁴.
E<sub>molar</sub> = 2.461 × 10⁵ J/mol = 246.1 kJ/mol.
Sig figs: match the 4-figure photon energy. Final answer: 2.461 × 10⁵ J/mol (246.1 kJ/mol).

sections.heading: The Bohr model for hydrogen
paragraphs: Bohr's model for the hydrogen atom (one electron) says the electron can occupy only certain energy levels labeled by a positive integer n = 1, 2, 3, … The energy of level n is E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6 eV / n². The negative sign means the electron is bound. E = 0 at infinite separation (n → ∞).

When the electron drops from a higher level n<sub>high</sub> to a lower level n<sub>low</sub>, the atom emits a photon. The photon energy equals the gap: ΔE = E<sub>high</sub> − E<sub>low</sub> (take the positive difference for the photon).
The Balmer series is the set of drops that end at n = 2. The famous red line is n = 3 → 2 at about 656 nm. The blue-green line is n = 4 → 2 at 486 nm.

Absorption is the reverse of emission. The electron jumps up when the atom absorbs a photon whose energy matches a level gap. Only those matching energies are absorbed strongly, which is why hydrogen's absorption spectrum shows sharp lines.
Bohr's model works quantitatively for hydrogen-like species (one electron): H, He⁺, Li²⁺. For He⁺ the energies scale by Z²: E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6 Z² / n² eV with Z = 2.

The ground state is n = 1. Any n ≥ 2 is an excited state. When n → ∞, the electron is free and the atom is ionized. The ionization energy of H from the ground state is 13.6 eV, which equals −E<sub>1</sub>.

figure.alt: Bohr energy-level diagram for hydrogen showing n=1, 2, 3 and infinity, with a red emission arrow for the Balmer n=3 to n=2 photon at 656 nm.

worked.title: Photon energy for the n = 3 → 2 transition (in eV)
steps: Write E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6 eV / n².
The electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2, so it loses energy. The photon carries that lost energy.

Photon energy E<sub>photon</sub> = E<sub>3</sub> − E<sub>2</sub>? Careful: E<sub>3</sub> is less negative than E<sub>2</sub>, so E<sub>3</sub> − E<sub>2</sub> is positive: (−13.6/9) − (−13.6/4) = −13.6/9 + 13.6/4.
Factor: E<sub>photon</sub> = 13.6 (1/4 − 1/9) eV.
Common denominator: 1/4 − 1/9 = 9/36 − 4/36 = 5/36.
Final answer: 1.89 eV (3 sig figs from 13.6).

workedExamples.title: Wavelength of the n = 3 → 2 line with the Rydberg formula
steps: Rydberg formula for hydrogen: 1/λ = R<sub>H</sub> (1/n<sub>low</sub>² − 1/n<sub>high</sub>²), with R<sub>H</sub> = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.
Here n<sub>low</sub> = 2, n<sub>high</sub> = 3.
Final answer: 656.3 nm (the red Balmer line).

mistake.wrong: Computing E<sub>photon</sub> as E<sub>2</sub> − E<sub>3</sub> and reporting a negative energy for the emitted light.
mistake.whyWrong: Photon energy is a positive amount of energy carried by the light. E<sub>2</sub> is more negative than E<sub>3</sub>, so E<sub>2</sub> − E<sub>3</sub> is negative and is not the photon energy.
mistake.correct: Take the positive gap: E<sub>photon</sub> = |E<sub>high</sub> − E<sub>low</sub>| = 13.6 (1/n<sub>low</sub>² − 1/n<sub>high</sub>²) eV for emission.

sections.heading: Quantum numbers
paragraphs: Modern quantum theory replaces Bohr orbits with orbitals. Four quantum numbers label an electron in an atom:
1. Principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, … It sets the shell and the main energy scale.
2. Angular-momentum quantum number ℓ = 0, 1, 2, …, (n − 1). It sets the subshell shape. Names: ℓ = 0 is s, 1 is p, 2 is d, 3 is f.
3. Magnetic quantum number m<sub>ℓ</sub> = −ℓ, …, 0, …, +ℓ. It labels the orientation of the orbital. An s subshell has 1 orbital. A p subshell has 3. A d subshell has 5.
4. Spin quantum number m<sub>s</sub> = +½ or −½. Each orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle).
The set (n, ℓ, m<sub>ℓ</sub>) labels one orbital. The set (n, ℓ, m<sub>ℓ</sub>, m<sub>s</sub>) labels one electron in that orbital.
Shell capacity: shell n holds at most 2n² electrons. So n = 1 holds 2, n = 2 holds 8, n = 3 holds 18. That matches the familiar 2, 8, 18 pattern.
Forbidden combinations are common trap answers on exams. Examples: n = 1 with ℓ = 1 (no 1p); n = 2 with ℓ = 2 (no 2d); m<sub>ℓ</sub> = 2 when ℓ = 1 (m<sub>ℓ</sub> cannot exceed ℓ).

worked.title: Allowed quantum numbers for a 2p electron
steps: For any 2p electron, n = 2 (the shell number in the label).
p means ℓ = 1.
m<sub>ℓ</sub> for ℓ = 1 can be −1, 0, or +1.
m<sub>s</sub> can be +½ or −½.
One valid set is n = 2, ℓ = 1, m<sub>ℓ</sub> = 0, m<sub>s</sub> = +½.
A forbidden example: n = 2, ℓ = 2 is impossible because ℓ must be less than n (ℓ max = n − 1 = 1).

workedExamples.title: How many electrons can fit in n = 3?
steps: Use capacity 2n² with n = 3.
Broken down by subshell: 3s (1 orbital, 2 e⁻) + 3p (3 orbitals, 6 e⁻) + 3d (5 orbitals, 10 e⁻) = 18.
Final answer: 18 electrons.

sections.heading: Orbital shapes
paragraphs: An orbital is a region of space where an electron is likely to be found. The shape comes from the wavefunction for that (n, ℓ, m<sub>ℓ</sub>).

An s orbital is spherical. A p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus (a dumbbell). Many d orbitals have four lobes (a cloverleaf). The figure below shows the common schematic shapes for 1s, 2p, and a 3d orbital.
Nodes are places where the electron density is zero. A 2s orbital has a spherical node inside. A 2p orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus.
The sign labels (+/−) on orbital lobes are the sign of the wavefunction, not electric charge. Overlap of same-sign lobes builds bonding interactions later in the bonding chapters.
Do not picture an electron traveling on a Bohr ring when you use orbitals. The orbital picture replaces that ring with a probability cloud.

figure.alt: Schematic orbital shapes: spherical 1s, dumbbell 2p with plus and minus lobes, and a four-leaf 3d clover (dx2−y2 style).

sections.why: Orbital shapes matter later for bonding: which orbitals overlap, and at what angle, sets molecular geometry.

sections.heading: Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund
paragraphs: A ground-state electron configuration lists how electrons fill orbitals in an atom at lowest energy. Three rules guide the filling:
1. Aufbau (building-up): fill lower-energy orbitals before higher ones. A common order is 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p …
2. Pauli exclusion: no two electrons in an atom can share the same four quantum numbers. Practical result: an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.
3. Hund's rule: when electrons occupy degenerate orbitals (same energy, like the three 2p orbitals), put one electron in each orbital with parallel spins before pairing any of them.
Degenerate means equal in energy. The three 2p orbitals are degenerate in a free atom. Hund's rule applies to any set of degenerate orbitals (2p, 3p, 3d, …).
A box diagram draws one box per orbital and arrows for electrons (↑ and ↓ for the two spins). Empty box = empty orbital. One arrow = unpaired. Two arrows = paired.

Why Hund's rule exists in plain terms: electrons repel each other. Spreading them across different orbitals (with the same spin) keeps them farther apart on average than pairing them in one orbital. That arrangement is lower in energy.
Pauli's rule is absolute. Hund and Aufbau describe the lowest-energy arrangement; excited atoms can violate Aufbau temporarily when light pumps an electron up.
After you finish a box diagram, count the arrows. The number of arrows must equal Z for a neutral atom, or Z minus the positive charge (or Z plus the negative charge size) for an ion.
sections.why: These three rules let you write the ground-state configuration for almost any main-group or first-row transition element without memorizing each one separately.

figure.alt: Orbital box diagrams for carbon (1s2 2s2 2p2 with two unpaired 2p electrons) and nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3 with three unpaired 2p electrons) illustrating Hund’s rule.

worked.title: Orbital diagram for carbon and nitrogen
steps: Carbon has Z = 6, so 6 electrons total.
Fill the lowest orbital first: 1s takes 2 electrons with opposite spins. Write 1s².
Next is 2s: put 2 electrons with opposite spins. Write 2s². Electrons used so far: 4. Remaining: 2.
Next is 2p. There are three 2p orbitals of equal energy.
Hund's rule: place the first remaining electron in one 2p orbital (say 2p<sub>x</sub>). Place the second in a different 2p orbital (2p<sub>y</sub>), with the same spin direction as the first.
Do not pair both electrons in 2p<sub>x</sub>. That would cost pairing energy and break Hund's rule.
Carbon configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p², with two unpaired 2p electrons.
Nitrogen has Z = 7. Same filling through 1s² 2s² leaves 3 electrons for the 2p subshell.
Place one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals with parallel spins: 1s² 2s² 2p³, three unpaired electrons.

sections.heading: Writing configurations and noble-gas shorthand
paragraphs: The full configuration lists every subshell. Noble-gas shorthand replaces the inner core with the symbol of the previous noble gas in brackets, then writes only the remaining electrons.
Example: Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹, which shortens to [Ne] 3s¹. The electrons after the noble-gas core are the valence electrons for main-group elements.
The block of the periodic table matches the last subshell being filled: s-block (Groups 1–2), p-block (Groups 13–18), d-block (transition metals), f-block (lanthanides and actinides).
Period number matches the highest n in the configuration for main-group elements. Na ends in 3s¹ and sits in Period 3. Cl ends in 3p⁵ and also sits in Period 3.
Group number for main-group elements relates to valence electron count. Na has 1 valence electron (Group 1). Cl has 7 valence electrons (Group 17 in the IUPAC numbering).

Order of writing vs order of filling: electrons fill 4s before 3d in Aufbau, but many texts write the configuration in order of increasing n (… 3d then 4s) for ions. For neutral atoms, writing Aufbau order (4s before 3d) or n-order (3d before 4s) are both accepted if the electron counts are correct.
Condensed tip: after you write a configuration, add the superscripts. If the sum is not Z, you missed or double-counted a subshell.
Calcium check: Ca (Z = 20) is [Ar] 4s². It sits in Period 4, Group 2, s-block. If your configuration for Ca ends in 3d or 4p, the electron count or Aufbau order is wrong.

Valence vs core: for main-group atoms the valence electrons are those beyond the previous noble-gas core. Those are the electrons that take part in bonding. Core electrons stay put in ordinary chemical reactions.

worked.title: Identify the element [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³
steps: Kr is krypton, Z = 36. Everything in brackets is the Kr core.
Count electrons written after Kr: 4d¹⁰ adds 10, 5s² adds 2, 5p³ adds 3. Total added = 15.
Atomic number of the element = 36 + 15 = 51.
Z = 51 is antimony, Sb.
Check on the table: Period 5, Group 15 (the nitrogen family). The last subshell is 5p, so it sits in the p-block. That matches Sb.
Final answer: Sb (antimony).

workedExamples.title: Write the ground-state configuration of S (Z = 16)
steps: Fill in order: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.
Check the electron count: 2+2+6+2+4 = 16. Good.
Noble-gas shorthand: neon is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, so S is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴.
Final answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, or [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴.

sections.heading: Cr and Cu exceptions
paragraphs: Two first-row exceptions appear in almost every textbook. Chromium and copper prefer a half-filled or filled d subshell over the strict Aufbau prediction.
Cr (Z = 24): the expected [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴ is higher in energy than the observed [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵. Half-filled 3d⁵ is especially stable.
Cu (Z = 29): the expected [Ar] 4s² 3d⁹ is higher than the observed [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. A filled 3d¹⁰ is especially stable.
Memorize these two. Do not invent other exceptions unless a problem or table says so.

After Cr and Cu, later exceptions exist in heavier transition metals, but intro courses usually test Cr and Cu only. When in doubt on an exam, apply Aufbau unless the element is Cr or Cu (or the problem states an exception).
Mo and Ag show similar patterns to Cr and Cu in some tables, but your first priority is Cr and Cu.
A memory hook many students use: half-full (d⁵) and full (d¹⁰) d subshells are worth "stealing" one s electron. Cr steals to make d⁵. Cu steals to make d¹⁰.

figure.alt: Orbital box diagrams for chromium as [Ar] 3d5 4s1 with six unpaired electrons, and for Fe3+ as [Ar] 3d5 with five unpaired 3d electrons.

worked.title: Ground-state configuration of Cr
steps: Z(Cr) = 24. Argon core is 18 electrons, so 6 remain.
Strict Aufbau would suggest 4s² 3d⁴.
Apply the chromium exception: move one electron from 4s into 3d to make 3d⁵ 4s¹.
Write [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (order of writing 3d before 4s in the final label is common for transition metals; either 4s¹ 3d⁵ or 3d⁵ 4s¹ is understood).
Orbital picture: five unpaired 3d electrons and one unpaired 4s electron → six unpaired electrons total.

workedExamples.title: Ground-state configuration of Cu
steps: Z(Cu) = 29. Argon core = 18. Electrons left = 11.
Strict Aufbau would suggest 4s² 3d⁹.
Apply the copper exception: one electron moves from 4s to 3d to complete 3d¹⁰.
Write [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰ (or [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹).
Unpaired electrons: only the single 4s electron is unpaired (3d¹⁰ is fully paired).
Final answer: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰.

sections.heading: Configurations of ions
paragraphs: For main-group ions, add or remove valence electrons from the neutral configuration. O is [He] 2s² 2p⁴. O²⁻ is [He] 2s² 2p⁶, which is the same as Ne.
For transition-metal cations, remove the s electrons before the d electrons. Neutral Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶. Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
Why s before d: in the ion, the 3d orbitals drop below 4s, so the 4s electrons are the ones lost first when the atom is ionized.
Isoelectronic warning: Na⁺, Ne, and F⁻ all have the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Same electron arrangement does not mean same size or same ionization energy; those still depend on nuclear charge.
When a problem asks for the number of unpaired electrons in an ion, draw the orbital boxes after you write the ion configuration. Do not use the neutral atom's unpaired count.
Main-group anion example: Cl is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵. Cl⁻ adds one electron to finish 3p⁶: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶, same as Ar. That is why chloride is a closed-shell, noble-gas-like ion.
Same method for Mn²⁺ (Z = 25): neutral Mn is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵; Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons. Always rebuild the ion from the neutral atom rather than guessing the d count.

worked.title: Configuration of Fe³⁺
steps: Neutral Fe (Z = 26): [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.
Fe³⁺ has lost 3 electrons.
Remove the two 4s electrons first: that accounts for 2 of the 3.
Remove one more electron from 3d: 3d⁶ → 3d⁵.
Fe³⁺ configuration: [Ar] 3d⁵.
This is a half-filled d subshell with five unpaired electrons.

workedExamples.title: Configuration of Cu⁺
steps: Neutral Cu is the exception: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰.
Cu⁺ loses the 4s electron.
Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰.
Final answer: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ (diamagnetic, no unpaired electrons).

mistake.wrong: Writing Fe³⁺ as [Ar] 4s² 3d³ by stripping three electrons from 3d and leaving 4s alone.
mistake.whyWrong: Transition-metal cations lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons. Leaving 4s² while emptying 3d reverses the real ionization order.
mistake.correct: Start from Fe [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Remove 4s² first, then one 3d electron → [Ar] 3d⁵.

sections.heading: Atomic radius and effective nuclear charge
paragraphs: Atomic radius is a measure of atom size. Across a period (left to right), atomic radius generally decreases. Down a group, atomic radius generally increases.

Why across a period: each step adds a proton to the nucleus and an electron to the same valence shell. The stronger nuclear pull wins, so the shell shrinks. Chemists describe this with effective nuclear charge Z<sub>eff</sub>: the net positive pull felt by a valence electron after inner electrons shield some of the full nuclear charge Z.
Why down a group: each step adds a new shell (larger n). The outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus, so the atom is larger even though Z is also larger.
There is more than one experimental definition of radius (covalent, metallic, van der Waals). The periodic trends taught here are the same qualitative pattern for all of them.

Effective nuclear charge for a valence electron is often estimated as Z<sub>eff</sub> ≈ Z − S, where S is a shielding constant from the inner electrons. Across Period 2, Z<sub>eff</sub> rises steadily, which is why atoms shrink.
Noble-gas radii are often van der Waals radii and look large on some charts; compare like with like when you read a figure. For metals, metallic radii are the usual comparison down a group.
Transition-metal radii change more slowly across a period than main-group radii because added electrons enter an inner d subshell and shield each other strongly.
sections.why: Radius trends explain bond lengths, ion sizes, and why lattice energies and hydration energies change across the table.

worked.title: Which is larger, Na or Cl? Na or K?
steps: Na and Cl are in the same period (Period 3). Na is on the left (Group 1). Cl is on the right (Group 17).
Across a period, Z<sub>eff</sub> rises and radius falls. Prediction: Na is larger than Cl.
Na and K are in the same group (Group 1). K is in Period 4, below Na in Period 3.
Down a group, a new shell is added. Prediction: K is larger than Na.
Quick Z<sub>eff</sub> check for Na vs Cl: both have Ne-like cores, but Cl has Z = 17 while Na has Z = 11, so Cl's valence electrons feel a stronger pull.
Final answers: radius Na > Cl; radius K > Na.

sections.heading: Ionic radius
paragraphs: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms because they have lost the outer shell (or lost electrons from it) and the remaining electrons feel a stronger pull per electron. Anions are larger than their parent atoms because extra electrons increase electron–electron repulsion and the same nuclear charge is spread over more electrons.
Isoelectronic ions have the same number of electrons. For an isoelectronic set, the ion with the most protons is the smallest, because Z is highest while the electron count is fixed.
For a single element, radius order is usually anion > neutral atom > cation. Example for oxygen: O²⁻ > O > O⁺ (O⁺ is uncommon in simple compounds but the size idea holds).
When comparing ions that are not isoelectronic, you need both electron count and nuclear charge. Prefer isoelectronic comparisons when the problem allows them.
The schematic chart in this section shows the isoelectronic set O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ drawn larger to smaller. It is a teaching sketch, not a scale drawing of measured picometers.

worked.title: Order Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ by increasing radius
steps: Count electrons for each ion.
Na⁺: Na has Z = 11; Na⁺ has 10 electrons.
Mg²⁺: Mg has Z = 12; Mg²⁺ has 10 electrons.
F⁻: F has Z = 9; F⁻ has 10 electrons.
O²⁻: O has Z = 8; O²⁻ has 10 electrons.
All four are isoelectronic with Ne (10 electrons).
Compare nuclear charge Z: Mg 12 > Na 11 > F 9 > O 8.
Higher Z pulls the same 10 electrons closer, so the radius is smaller.
Order of increasing radius: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻.

workedExamples.title: Which is larger, Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺?
steps: Both ions come from Fe (Z = 26).
Fe²⁺ has 24 electrons. Fe³⁺ has 23 electrons.
Fe³⁺ has the same nuclear charge but fewer electrons, so electron–electron repulsion is lower and Z<sub>eff</sub> per electron is higher.
Fe³⁺ is smaller than Fe²⁺.
Final answer: Fe²⁺ > Fe³⁺ in radius.

mistake.wrong: Ordering the isoelectronic set by atomic number of the element alone without checking the electron count, or ranking by the ion charge sign only (all anions bigger than all cations is true here, but that shortcut fails when charges differ within cations).
mistake.whyWrong: The reliable rule for isoelectronic ions is: more protons → smaller ion. Charge sign is a clue, but the proton count is the reason.
mistake.correct: Confirm the ions share the same electron count, then sort by Z. Here Mg²⁺ (Z=12) is smallest and O²⁻ (Z=8) is largest.

sections.heading: Ionization energy
paragraphs: First ionization energy (IE₁) is the energy needed to remove the highest-energy electron from 1 mol of gas-phase atoms: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. IE₁ generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Across a period: Z<sub>eff</sub> rises, so electrons are held more tightly. Down a group: the outer electron is farther from the nucleus, so it is easier to remove.

Two famous Period 2 exceptions: Be → B and N → O. IE₁ of B is lower than Be because B starts a new 2p subshell (higher energy, less tightly held) while Be has a filled 2s². IE₁ of O is lower than N because O must pair two electrons in one 2p orbital; the pairing repulsion makes that electron easier to remove than an unpaired 2p electron in N.

Second ionization energy IE₂ is the energy to remove a second electron from the already positive ion: X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻. IE₂ is always larger than IE₁ because you are pulling an electron away from a more positive species.

A huge jump between IE₁ and IE₂ (or between IE₂ and IE₃) signals that you have broken into a noble-gas core. Na has a low IE₁ and a very high IE₂, which matches forming Na⁺ but not Na²⁺ in ordinary chemistry.

Removing successive electrons always costs more energy: IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃ < … for a given element. The jumps are modest while you remove valence electrons and become huge when you start removing core electrons.
Metals tend to have low IE₁ (they form cations easily). Nonmetals tend to have high IE₁ (they hold electrons tightly and more often form anions or share electrons).

worked.title: Why is IE₁(O) less than IE₁(N)?
steps: Write the valence configurations: N is 2s² 2p³. O is 2s² 2p⁴.
In N, the three 2p electrons sit one in each 2p orbital (Hund). No pairs in 2p.
In O, four 2p electrons mean one of the 2p orbitals holds a pair.
The paired electrons repel each other. That repulsion raises the energy of the electron you remove from O.
So less energy is needed to remove one electron from O than from N, even though O has a higher nuclear charge.
Result: IE₁ dips from N to O on the Period 2 plot.

workedExamples.title: Rank IE₁ for Na, Mg, Al
steps: All are Period 3. General trend: IE₁ rises left → right, but watch the Mg → Al exception (like Be → B).
Na is 3s¹. Mg is 3s². Al is 3s² 3p¹.
Mg has a filled 3s² subshell. Al starts the 3p subshell.
IE₁ order: Na < Al < Mg. (Al is below Mg because of the p-subshell start; both are above Na.)
Final answer: Na has the lowest IE₁ of the three; Mg has the highest.

sections.heading: Electron affinity and magnetism
paragraphs: Electron affinity (EA) is the energy change when a gas-phase atom gains an electron: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). A more negative EA means a more exothermic (favorable) gain. Halogens have very negative electron affinities. Noble gases have EA near zero or positive (unfavorable).

Paramagnetism and diamagnetism come from unpaired electrons. A species with one or more unpaired electrons is paramagnetic (attracted into a magnetic field). A species with all electrons paired is diamagnetic (weakly repelled).

To decide, write the ground-state configuration or orbital diagram and count unpaired electrons. Ca is [Ar] 4s² → 0 unpaired → diamagnetic. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ → in the high-spin free-ion picture used in intro chemistry, four unpaired → paramagnetic. Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ → 0 unpaired → diamagnetic.

Sign caution: some older tables report electron affinity as a positive number meaning "energy released." Modern thermochemical tables usually report ΔE for X(g)+e⁻→X⁻(g) as a negative value when the process is exothermic. Read the sign convention in the problem.

In coordination chemistry, Fe²⁺ can be high-spin or low-spin depending on the ligands. Intro general chemistry almost always means the free-ion high-spin count (four unpaired for 3d⁶) when it asks about Fe²⁺ paramagnetism.

Fluorine's electron affinity is slightly less negative than chlorine's in many tables, even though F is more electronegative. The small F atom packs electron–electron repulsion into a tight space when it forms F⁻. That detail is optional for early exams; the main pattern is that halogens have the most favorable (most negative) EA values.

Magnetism check procedure: (1) write the configuration of the species asked, (2) draw the valence orbital boxes with Hund's rule, (3) count unpaired arrows. Zero means diamagnetic. One or more means paramagnetic.

figure.alt: Orbital boxes showing Ca ([Ar] 4s2) and Zn2+ ([Ar] 3d10) with zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic), and Fe2+ ([Ar] 3d6) with four unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).

worked.title: Is Fe²⁺ paramagnetic?
steps: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶.
Place six electrons in five 3d orbitals with Hund's rule: one in each of five orbitals first (5 electrons), then pair the sixth in one orbital.
Unpaired count: 4 (five orbitals start with one each; pairing removes one unpaired, leaving four unpaired).
Four unpaired electrons means Fe²⁺ is paramagnetic.
Final answer: paramagnetic (4 unpaired electrons in the free-ion orbital diagram).

workedExamples.title: Ca vs Zn²⁺ vs Fe²⁺ magnetism
steps: Ca: [Ar] 4s². The 4s box has two paired electrons. Unpaired = 0 → diamagnetic.
Zn²⁺: Zn is [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰; Zn²⁺ loses 4s² → [Ar] 3d¹⁰. All five 3d boxes paired. Unpaired = 0 → diamagnetic.
Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶. High-spin free-ion boxes: ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ then pair one → four unpaired.
Unpaired = 4 → paramagnetic.
Final answers: Ca diamagnetic; Zn²⁺ diamagnetic; Fe²⁺ paramagnetic.

sections.heading: Lewis structures
paragraphs: A Lewis structure shows valence electrons as dots and bonding pairs as lines. It is a bookkeeping tool for how atoms share or transfer electrons in a molecule or ion.
A reliable build path:
1. Sum the valence electrons for all atoms. For an anion, add electrons equal to the charge. For a cation, subtract electrons equal to the charge.
2. Choose a skeleton. The least electronegative atom (not hydrogen) is usually central. Connect each outer atom with a single bond (that uses 2 electrons per bond).
3. Complete octets on the outer atoms (H wants only 2 electrons, a duet).
4. Place any leftover electrons on the central atom as lone pairs.
5. If the central atom still lacks an octet, convert lone pairs from outer atoms into multiple bonds.
6. Check formal charges and adjust for better structures when needed.

Formal charge on an atom = (valence electrons in the free atom) − (nonbonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). The best Lewis structures usually keep formal charges small, put negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, and keep the sum of formal charges equal to the ion charge (or zero for a molecule).
Beyond the octet: period-3 and heavier atoms (P, S, Cl, …) can expand their octets when needed (as in SF₄ and PCl₅). Be and B often have incomplete octets in stable molecules (BF₃).

Electronegativity (tendency to attract bonding electrons) helps you judge bond polarity and which atom should carry a negative formal charge. Fluorine is the most electronegative element. The scale rises toward the upper right of the main-group table (ignoring noble gases).
sections.why: Every later shape, polarity, and bond-enthalpy estimate starts from a correct electron count and skeleton. A wrong Lewis structure poisons the rest.

figure.alt: Lewis structures of H2O (bent, two lone pairs on oxygen), CO2 (linear O=C=O), and SF4 (sulfur with four F bonds and one lone pair); all formal charges zero.

worked.title: Lewis structure of H₂O
steps: Valence electrons: H has 1 each, O has 6. Total = 1 + 1 + 6 = 8.
Skeleton: H–O–H (O is central; H is never central).
Two O–H single bonds use 4 electrons. Electrons left = 8 − 4 = 4.
Place the remaining 4 electrons on oxygen as two lone pairs.
Check octets/duets: each H has 2 electrons. O has 4 bonding + 4 nonbonding = 8. Good.
Formal charge on O: 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Each H: 1 − 0 − ½(2) = 0.
Final: bent Lewis structure with two lone pairs on oxygen; all formal charges zero.

workedExamples.title: Lewis structure of CO₂
steps: Valence electrons: C = 4, each O = 6. Total = 4 + 12 = 16.
Skeleton: O–C–O.
Two single bonds use 4 electrons. Left = 12.
Complete octets on both O atoms first: each O needs 6 more electrons as lone pairs → that uses all 12. Central C then has only 4 electrons.
C lacks an octet. Form a double bond to one O by moving one O lone pair into a C=O bond. C now has 6 electrons; still short.
Form a second double bond to the other O. Structure: O=C=O.
Formal charges: each O is 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. C is 4 − 0 − ½(8) = 0.
Final: linear O=C=O with all formal charges zero.

sections.heading: Resonance and formal charge
paragraphs: Sometimes one Lewis structure is not enough. Resonance structures are two or more Lewis drawings that differ only in electron placement, not in atom positions. The real molecule is a hybrid of them. Double-headed arrows link resonance forms.
Classic example: ozone, O₃. One Lewis form has a double bond on the left and a single bond on the right; the other form swaps them. The real O–O bonds are equal and intermediate.
Use formal charge to rank resonance forms. Prefer forms with formal charges closest to zero. Prefer negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom.

Do not average resonance forms that have very different formal-charge quality. A form with large separated charges contributes less than a form with all zeros. Still draw major forms when they are equivalent, as in nitrate and ozone.

worked.title: Formal charges in the nitrate ion NO₃⁻
steps: Valence electrons: N = 5, three O = 18, plus 1 for the 1− charge → total 24.
Skeleton: N central, three O around it. Three single bonds use 6 electrons. Left = 18.
Complete octets on the three O atoms (6 electrons each as lone pairs) uses all 18. N then has only 6 electrons.
Make one N=O double bond by moving an O lone pair. Now N has an octet.
In that form: the double-bonded O has formal charge 6 − 4 − ½(4) = 0. Each single-bonded O has 6 − 6 − ½(2) = −1. N has 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1.
Sum of formal charges = +1 − 1 − 1 + 0 = −1, matching the ion charge.
There are three equivalent resonance forms (the double bond can sit toward any of the three O atoms). The real ion has three equal N–O bonds.

sections.heading: VSEPR shapes and polarity
paragraphs: VSEPR (valence-shell electron-pair repulsion) says electron domains around a central atom spread out to minimize repulsion. A domain is a lone pair, a single bond, a double bond, or a triple bond. Multiple bonds count as one domain for shape.
Electron-domain geometries: 2 domains → linear; 3 → trigonal planar; 4 → tetrahedral; 5 → trigonal bipyramidal; 6 → octahedral.

Molecular shape names the atom positions only. Lone pairs still push and shrink bond angles. Examples: AX₂E (bent, from trigonal planar electron geometry); AX₃E (trigonal pyramidal); AX₂E₂ (bent, from tetrahedral); AX₄E (seesaw, from trigonal bipyramidal).
In trigonal bipyramidal arrangements, lone pairs prefer equatorial sites. That is why SF₄ is seesaw, not a different AX₄E isomer.

A molecule is polar if it has a nonzero net dipole. Bond dipoles point toward the more electronegative atom. If the shape is symmetric enough that bond dipoles cancel (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄), the molecule is nonpolar even if the bonds are polar. If dipoles do not cancel (H₂O, NH₃, SF₄), the molecule is polar.
sections.why: Shape and polarity control boiling points, solubility, and how molecules pack. VSEPR is the fast prediction tool before you meet hybridization.

figure.alt: Three-dimensional seesaw shape of SF4 from trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry with an equatorial lone pair, and a net dipole arrow showing the molecule is polar.

worked.title: Shape and polarity of SF₄
steps: Valence electrons: S = 6, each F = 7 → 6 + 28 = 34.
Skeleton: four S–F single bonds. That uses 8 electrons. Left = 26.
Complete octets on four F atoms: 4 × 6 = 24 electrons as F lone pairs. Left = 2 electrons → one lone pair on S.
Domains on S: 4 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair = 5 domains. Electron geometry: trigonal bipyramidal.
Place the lone pair equatorial. Molecular shape: seesaw (AX₄E).
The lone pair and the unsymmetric seesaw arrangement mean bond dipoles do not cancel.
Final answer: seesaw shape, polar molecule.

workedExamples.title: Shape and polarity of CO₂ vs SO₂
steps: CO₂: C has 2 domains (two double bonds). Electron geometry and shape: linear. Two C=O dipoles point opposite ways and cancel → nonpolar.
SO₂: S has 3 domains (two S–O bonding domains + one lone pair in the common Lewis/resonance picture). Electron geometry: trigonal planar. Shape: bent (AX₂E).
Bent shape → dipoles do not cancel → polar.
Final answers: CO₂ linear nonpolar; SO₂ bent polar.

mistake.wrong: Calling SF₄ tetrahedral because there are four F atoms attached to S, and then saying it is nonpolar like CCl₄.
mistake.whyWrong: Shape counting must include lone pairs on the central atom. SF₄ has five electron domains, not four. The seesaw shape is not tetrahedral, and its dipoles do not cancel.
mistake.correct: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom. For SF₄ that is 5 domains → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry → seesaw molecular shape → polar.

sections.heading: Bond enthalpies for reaction ΔH
paragraphs: Average bond enthalpy (bond energy) is the enthalpy needed to break one mole of a given type of bond in the gas phase. Tables list typical values in kJ/mol.

For a gas-phase reaction estimate: ΔH ≈ Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed). You pay energy to break bonds. You release energy when new bonds form (that is why formed bonds are subtracted).
This is an estimate. It uses average values, not the exact bond enthalpy in one specific molecule. It still gives the right sign and a useful size for many early problems.
Standard values used in the examples below (kJ/mol): H–H 436, O=O 498, O–H 463, C–H 412, C–C 348, C=C 614, C≡C 839, N≡N 944, H–Cl 431, Cl–Cl 242.

Bond enthalpy estimates assume gas-phase species. If a reaction involves liquids or solids, the estimate misses phase-change enthalpies. Still, for many exam problems the table values are what you are asked to use.

worked.title: Estimate ΔH for 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (gas)
steps: Bonds broken: 2 H–H and 1 O=O.
Bonds formed: each H₂O has 2 O–H bonds; two H₂O give 4 O–H bonds.
Energy released on forming: 4(463) = 1852 kJ.
ΔH ≈ 1370 − 1852 = −482 kJ for the reaction as written.
Sign check: negative means exothermic, which matches burning hydrogen in oxygen.
Final answer: about −482 kJ (estimate).

workedExamples.title: Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl
steps: Bonds broken: 1 H–H (436) + 1 Cl–Cl (242) = 678 kJ.
Bonds formed: 2 H–Cl = 2(431) = 862 kJ.
Final answer: about −184 kJ.

items.q: What is the formal charge on N in the best Lewis structure of NH₄⁺?
items.a: N has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs: FC = 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1. Each H is 0. Sum = +1, matching the charge.

items.q: Is CCl₄ polar or nonpolar?
