sections.heading: Hybridization
paragraphs: Valence-bond theory says a covalent bond forms when atomic orbitals on two atoms overlap and share an electron pair. Hybridization is a model that mixes atomic orbitals on one atom so the resulting hybrid orbitals point toward the domains VSEPR predicts.
Common hybrids: sp (2 domains, linear, 180°), sp² (3 domains, trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (4 domains, tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (5 domains, trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (6 domains, octahedral).

How to assign hybridization: draw the Lewis structure, count electron domains on the atom, then match the hybrid set to that count. The hybrid set uses one s orbital plus as many p (and d, when needed) orbitals as the domain count requires.
Example map: carbon in CH₄ has 4 domains → sp³. Carbon in H₂C=CH₂ has 3 domains → sp². Carbon in HC≡CH has 2 domains → sp. Oxygen in H₂O has 4 domains (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) → sp³.

Hybridization is a model, not a detector reading. It is chosen to match the observed or VSEPR geometry. If the electron geometry is tetrahedral, we say sp³ whether the atom is C in methane or O in water.

Lone pairs occupy hybrid orbitals too. In water, two sp³ hybrids hold O–H bonds and two hold lone pairs. The H–O–H angle is a bit less than 109.5° because lone pairs take more space than bonding pairs.

Carbon chemistry uses this map constantly. Alkane carbons (four single bonds) are sp³. Alkene carbons (three domains) are sp². Alkyne carbons (two domains) are sp. Functional-group atoms follow the same domain count.

Expanded octets on period-3 atoms need d orbitals in the simple hybrid model (sp³d, sp³d²). Some advanced treatments avoid d orbitals; for this course, match the hybrid label to the VSEPR domain count as your textbook does.
sections.why: Hybridization links Lewis/VSEPR geometry to orbital language. It is the bridge into σ and π bonding.

worked.title: Hybridization of each carbon in CH₂=CH–C≡N
steps: Draw the chain: H₂C=CH–C≡N.
Left carbon (CH₂=): attached to 2 H and double-bonded to the next C → 3 domains → sp².
Middle carbon (–CH=): attached to 1 H, double-bonded to left C, single-bonded to the next C → 3 domains → sp².
Cyano carbon (–C≡): triple-bonded to N and single-bonded to the middle C → 2 domains → sp.
Nitrogen in –C≡N: one triple bond domain + one lone pair → 2 domains → sp.
Final answer: carbons are sp², sp², sp (left to right); N is sp.

sections.heading: Sigma and pi bonds
paragraphs: A σ (sigma) bond has electron density along the line joining the two nuclei. End-to-end overlap of hybrids or of an s orbital with a hybrid makes a σ bond. Every single, double, and triple bond contains exactly one σ bond.
A π (pi) bond has electron density above and below (or beside) the internuclear axis. Side-to-side overlap of leftover p orbitals makes π bonds. A double bond = 1 σ + 1 π. A triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.

In ethene (H₂C=CH₂), each carbon is sp². The three sp² hybrids make the C–H and C–C σ framework. The leftover p orbital on each carbon overlaps to make the π bond. In ethyne (HC≡CH), each carbon is sp; two leftover p orbitals on each carbon make two π bonds.
Rotation about a single (σ) bond is usually easy. Rotation about a double bond breaks the π overlap, so cis–trans isomers around C=C can be stable at room temperature.

Count practice: benzene C₆H₆ has 6 C–C σ bonds in the ring, 6 C–H σ bonds, and a delocalized π system often counted as 3 π bonds in a simple Lewis picture (true MO description is delocalized around the ring).
A useful exam habit: first count how many pairs of atoms are directly connected (that is the σ count), then add π from each double (+1) and triple (+2).
In ethyne, the C–H bonds are σ overlaps of H 1s with C sp hybrids. The C–C σ bond is sp–sp. The two π bonds are side-on p–p overlaps.

figure.alt: Hybridization sketch of ethene (sp2 carbons, one sigma and one pi bond) beside ethyne (sp carbons, one sigma and two pi bonds), with sigma in blue and pi in red.

worked.title: σ and π bonds in CH₂=CH–C≡N
steps: Formula of CH₂=CH–C≡N is C₃H₃N. That means 3 C–H bonds.
Atom-to-atom connections: 3 C–H, one C=C, one C–C (between the alkene and the cyano carbon), and one C≡N. Total connections = 6.
Each connection includes exactly one σ bond → 6 σ bonds.
π extras: C=C contributes 1 π; C≡N contributes 2 π → 3 π bonds.
Final answer: 6 σ and 3 π.

workedExamples.title: σ and π count in CO₂
steps: CO₂ is O=C=O.
Two C=O connections → 2 σ bonds (one in each double bond).
Each double bond adds 1 π → 2 π bonds.
Final answer: 2 σ and 2 π.

mistake.wrong: Counting a double bond as two σ bonds, or a triple bond as three σ bonds.
mistake.whyWrong: Only the first bond between two atoms is a σ bond. The second and third bonds are π bonds from side-on p overlap.
mistake.correct: One σ per connected atom pair. Add one π for a double bond and two π for a triple bond.

sections.heading: Molecular orbital basics
paragraphs: Molecular orbital (MO) theory combines atomic orbitals from the whole molecule into new orbitals that belong to the molecule. Two atomic orbitals make one bonding MO (lower energy) and one antibonding MO (higher energy, marked with *).
Electrons fill MOs much like atomic orbitals: lowest energy first, Pauli limit of two electrons per MO, and Hund's rule for degenerate MOs.
Bond order = ½(number of bonding electrons − number of antibonding electrons). Higher bond order means a stronger, usually shorter bond. Bond order 0 means no stable bond (as in He₂).
For O₂ and F₂, the valence MO energy order commonly taught is: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. (For B₂, C₂, and N₂ the π2p level sits below σ2p. Use the order the problem or table gives.)
Bonding MOs concentrate electron density between nuclei and stabilize the molecule. Antibonding MOs have a node between nuclei and destabilize it when occupied.
A photoelectron spectrum or a textbook diagram tells you the energy order. Memorize the two common orders for period-2 diatomics: π below σ for B₂/C₂/N₂, and σ below π for O₂/F₂.
Paramagnetic means attracted into a magnetic field (unpaired electrons). Diamagnetic means weakly pushed out (all electrons paired). MO theory predicts which diatomic molecules are which.
Bond order can be fractional (as in O₂⁺ = 2.5). Lewis structures struggle with that; MO handles it naturally from electron counts.
sections.why: MO theory explains magnetism and fractional bond orders that Lewis structures cannot show cleanly, especially O₂.

sections.heading: MO diagrams for O₂ and relatives
paragraphs: O₂ has 12 valence electrons to place in the MO scheme. Filling with the O₂/F₂ order gives two electrons in the π* set. Those two π* electrons sit in different orbitals with parallel spins (Hund), so O₂ has two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.
Lewis structures of O₂ with all electrons paired miss that fact. Liquid oxygen sticking to a magnet is the classic classroom demo.
Related ions: remove an antibonding electron to make O₂⁺ (higher bond order). Add an electron to π* to make O₂⁻ (lower bond order).
Bond length and bond strength trends follow bond order when you compare O₂⁺, O₂, and O₂⁻: higher bond order → shorter and stronger bond.
F₂ has bond order 1 and is diamagnetic. N₂ has bond order 3 and is diamagnetic. Those MO results match the Lewis pictures, unlike O₂.
Writing the electron configuration for O₂: (σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(σ2p)²(π2p)⁴(π*2p)². The π* set holds two unpaired electrons.
Removing one π* electron (to O₂⁺) raises bond order. Adding one (to O₂⁻) lowers it. Adding two (to O₂²⁻, peroxide) drops bond order to 1.
Classroom check: a tube of liquid O₂ hangs between the poles of a strong magnet; liquid N₂ does not. Paramagnetism of O₂ is not a book quirk. You can see it.

figure.alt: Molecular orbital energy diagram for O2 with sigma 2p below pi 2p, two unpaired electrons in pi-star, bond order 2 and paramagnetism; notes compare O2+ (BO 2.5) and O2− (BO 1.5).

worked.title: Bond orders of O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻
steps: For O₂ with 12 valence electrons in the standard diagram: bonding electrons = 8, antibonding electrons = 4.
Bond order = ½(8 − 4) = 2.
O₂⁺ has 11 valence electrons: one fewer antibonding electron than O₂, so antibonding = 3, bonding = 8.
Bond order(O₂⁺) = ½(8 − 3) = 2.5.
O₂⁻ has 13 valence electrons: one more antibonding electron than O₂, so antibonding = 5, bonding = 8.
Bond order(O₂⁻) = ½(8 − 5) = 1.5.
Trend: O₂⁺ has the strongest/shortest bond of the three; O₂⁻ has the weakest/longest.
Final answers: 2, 2.5, and 1.5.

workedExamples.title: Is O₂ diamagnetic or paramagnetic?
steps: Fill the O₂ MO diagram through π* with 12 electrons.
The last two electrons occupy the two degenerate π* orbitals singly with parallel spins.
Unpaired electrons = 2.
Final answer: paramagnetic.

workedExamples.title: Bond order of N₂ (use π2p below σ2p)
steps: N₂ has 10 valence electrons.
Filling: (σ2s)²(σ*2s)²(π2p)⁴(σ2p)².
Bonding electrons = 8; antibonding = 2.
Bond order = ½(8 − 2) = 3.
Final answer: bond order 3 (matches the Lewis triple bond); all electrons paired → diamagnetic.

workedExamples.title: Bond order of peroxide ion O₂²⁻
steps: O₂²⁻ has 14 valence electrons (same count as F₂).
Bonding electrons still 8; antibonding electrons now 6.
Bond order = ½(8 − 6) = 1.
Final answer: bond order 1; all electrons paired → diamagnetic.

sections.heading: Types of intermolecular forces
paragraphs: Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are attractions between molecules (or between separate formula units). They are much weaker than the covalent or ionic bonds inside a molecule, but they control boiling point, melting point, vapor pressure, and solubility.

London dispersion forces exist in every substance. They come from temporary, instantaneous dipoles in electron clouds. Larger, more polarizable electron clouds give stronger dispersion. Longer contact area (straight chains vs balls) also strengthens dispersion.
Dipole–dipole forces act between permanent dipoles in polar molecules. The positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another.

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong dipole–dipole case: H bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule. It is unusually strong for an IMF and explains many odd boiling points (water, HF, NH₃).
Ion–dipole forces appear when ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents (NaCl in water). They are stronger than ordinary dipole–dipole forces.

All molecules have dispersion. Polar molecules add dipole–dipole. Molecules with H–N, H–O, or H–F add hydrogen bonding. When you rank substances, identify the strongest force present, then compare within that class.

Solubility rule of thumb: like dissolves like. Polar solvents (water) dissolve polar and ionic solutes. Nonpolar solvents (hexane) dissolve nonpolar solutes. Hydrogen bonding between solute and solvent helps a lot.
Dispersion forces grow quickly with size. Iodine is a solid at room temperature while fluorine is a gas, even though both are nonpolar X₂ molecules. The difference is polarizability.
Hydrogen bonding is still much weaker than a covalent O–H bond. It is strong among IMFs, not strong compared with intramolecular bonds.

Quick ranking recipe: (1) ionic lattices beat molecular IMFs for melting points; (2) among molecules, hydrogen bonding beats ordinary dipole–dipole; (3) dipole–dipole beats dispersion only when masses are similar; (4) when only dispersion remains, larger and less compact wins.
sections.why: If you can name the strongest IMF in a pure substance, you can usually rank boiling points and decide whether a solid, liquid, or gas is expected at room temperature.

worked.title: Boiling points: HF, Ne, HCl
steps: Ne is a noble-gas atom. Only dispersion forces. Very weak for such a small cloud → lowest boiling point.
HCl is polar. It has dipole–dipole forces plus dispersion. Stronger than Ne.
HF can hydrogen-bond (H on F attracted to F lone pairs). That IMF is stronger than ordinary dipole–dipole in HCl.
Order of boiling points: Ne < HCl < HF.
Final answer: Ne < HCl < HF.

workedExamples.title: Rank IMF strength: CH₄, NH₃, NaCl (as a solid lattice idea)
steps: CH₄ is nonpolar → only dispersion.
NH₃ is polar and has N–H bonds → hydrogen bonding (+ dispersion).
NaCl is ionic. Ion–ion attractions in the lattice are much stronger than molecular IMFs.
For molecular IMFs only among the first two: CH₄ < NH₃. NaCl's melting point is far higher than either boiling point.
Final answer: molecular IMF order CH₄ < NH₃; ionic NaCl is in a different, much stronger class.

sections.heading: Shape, mass, and dispersion
paragraphs: Among similar compounds, stronger IMFs raise boiling and melting points and lower vapor pressure at a given temperature.

For nonpolar molecules of similar shape, larger molar mass usually means a larger electron cloud and stronger dispersion. So boiling points often rise down a halogen family: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ (F₂ and Cl₂ are gases; Br₂ liquid; I₂ solid at room temperature).

Shape matters at fixed formula mass. A straight-chain alkane has more surface contact than a compact branched isomer. More contact → stronger dispersion → higher boiling point. Pentane boils higher than neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane).
Isomer boiling-point questions almost always hinge on surface area when the formula is the same and both isomers are nonpolar. Branched → more compact → lower boiling point.
For polar vs nonpolar isomers (for example diethyl ether vs 1-butanol), hydrogen bonding in the alcohol wins over ether dipole forces.
When two molecules have similar mass and similar polarity, look at hydrogen bonding next. Alcohols boil higher than ethers of similar mass.
Network solids and metals are not "IMF" stories. Diamond and quartz melt high because covalent networks hold atoms, not because of London forces.

figure.alt: Side-by-side carbon skeletons of straight-chain n-pentane and compact neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane), noting that more surface contact raises boiling point via stronger London forces.

worked.title: Why pentane boils higher than neopentane
steps: Both are C₅H₁₂. Same molar mass, both nonpolar → only dispersion forces.
n-Pentane is a long chain. Molecules can lie side by side with large contact area.
Neopentane is compact and nearly spherical. Contact area between neighbors is smaller.
Larger contact area → stronger London forces in pentane.
Stronger IMF → higher boiling point for pentane.
Final answer: pentane has stronger dispersion from greater surface contact.

mistake.wrong: Ranking boiling points only by molar mass and ignoring hydrogen bonding or shape (for example predicting H₂O boils lower than H₂S because O is lighter than S).
mistake.whyWrong: Water's hydrogen bonding outweighs the mass trend that works for H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te. Mass is only one factor.
mistake.correct: Name the strongest IMF first. Then use mass and shape inside the same IMF class.

sections.heading: Vapor pressure and Clausius–Clapeyron
paragraphs: Vapor pressure is the pressure of a vapor in equilibrium with its liquid (or solid) at a fixed temperature. Stronger IMFs hold molecules in the liquid more tightly, so vapor pressure is lower at the same T.
Vapor pressure rises as temperature rises. More molecules have enough energy to escape.

The Clausius–Clapeyron equation links two vapor-pressure points: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔHvap / R) (1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Temperatures must be in kelvin. R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when ΔHvap is in J/mol (or use 8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ with ΔH in kJ/mol).
Boiling point is the temperature where vapor pressure equals external pressure. Normal boiling point uses 1 atm (or 1 bar, depending on the table).
A liquid with high vapor pressure at room temperature is volatile. Weak IMFs → high vapor pressure → low boiling point.

When you solve Clausius–Clapeyron for ΔH<sub>vap</sub>, rearrange: ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = −R × ln(P₂/P₁) / (1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Keep the sign of the temperature term straight so ΔH<sub>vap</sub> comes out positive for vaporization.
Plotting ln P against 1/T gives a straight line with slope −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R for a limited range. That is the two-point Clausius–Clapeyron idea in graph form.
Units reminder: if ΔHvap is 40.7 kJ/mol, either convert to 40700 J/mol and use R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹, or keep 40.7 kJ/mol and use R = 0.008314 kJ·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.
Boiling happens throughout the liquid when vapor pressure equals external pressure. Evaporation happens only at the surface and can occur below the boiling point.

worked.title: Find P₂ if P₁ = 1.00 atm at T₁ = 373 K, ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.7 kJ/mol, T₂ = 363 K
steps: This is water near its normal boiling point. ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.7 kJ/mol = 4.07 × 10⁴ J/mol.
Write ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.
Sig figs: report about 0.697 atm (vapor pressure falls as T falls below the boiling point).
Final answer: P₂ ≈ 0.697 atm.

workedExamples.title: Does vapor pressure rise or fall when IMF strength rises at fixed T?
steps: Stronger IMFs hold molecules in the liquid more tightly.
Fewer molecules escape to vapor at equilibrium.
Vapor pressure is lower.
Final answer: vapor pressure falls as IMF strength rises (at fixed T).

sections.heading: Phases and phase diagrams (intro)
paragraphs: Solid, liquid, and gas are the common phases for a pure substance. Heating can melt a solid or boil a liquid. Cooling reverses those changes.

A phase diagram plots pressure vs temperature and shows which phase is stable. Curves are equilibria between two phases. The triple point is where solid, liquid, and gas coexist. The critical point ends the liquid–gas curve; beyond it you cannot tell liquid from gas.
Reading tip: at a given P and T, the region you land in is the stable phase. Crossing a curve means a phase change at equilibrium.
Along the solid–gas curve, solid and vapor coexist (sublimation/deposition). Dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimes at 1 atm because that pressure is below CO₂'s triple-point pressure.
Critical temperature is the highest T at which a liquid can exist. Above T<sub>c</sub>, no amount of pressure liquefies the gas into a separate liquid phase.

Heating a solid at constant pressure: temperature rises until the melting curve, then stays (ideally) at the melting point while solid and liquid coexist, then rises again in the liquid region until boiling.

The slope of the solid–liquid line is steep. For water it leans slightly left (ice is less dense than liquid water), which is unusual and explains pressure melting under ice skates in the classic story, though friction also matters.

worked.title: What happens when you raise T at fixed P below the critical pressure?
steps: Start in the solid region at low T.
Warm at constant P: you cross the solid–liquid (melting) curve → liquid.
Warm further: you cross the liquid–gas (boiling/vaporization) curve → gas.
If instead your fixed P is below the triple-point pressure for that substance, heating the solid can sublime directly to gas without a stable liquid.
Final answer: solid → liquid → gas when P is between the triple and critical pressures.

workedExamples.title: Why does sweating cool you?
steps: Sweat is mostly water on the skin.
Evaporation is endothermic: the fastest molecules leave as vapor and take energy with them.
The remaining liquid and the skin lose thermal energy → temperature falls.
Final answer: evaporative cooling from vaporization of water.

sections.heading: Empirical gas laws
paragraphs: Gases are mostly empty space. Their volume, pressure, temperature, and amount are linked by simple laws when the gas behaves ideally.
Boyle's law: at fixed n and T, P is inversely proportional to V. PV = constant. Double the pressure, halve the volume.
Charles's law: at fixed n and P, V is proportional to absolute temperature T in kelvin. V/T = constant. Use kelvin, never °C alone, in gas equations.
Avogadro's law: at fixed T and P, V is proportional to n. Equal volumes of ideal gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of moles.
Convert °C to K with T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. For three-sig-fig work, 25.0 °C → 298.2 K is fine; many problems use 298 K.
A combined form without n: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ for a fixed amount of ideal gas. Cancel any quantity that does not change.

Standard temperature and pressure (STP) in many intro texts is 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atm. At STP, one mole of ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L. (Some modern tables use 1 bar; use the definition your problem states.)
Boyle in lab language: a syringe of trapped air shrinks when you push the plunger (raise P). Charles: a balloon shrinks in a freezer (lower T at nearly fixed P).
Always convert Celsius to kelvin before any gas equation. Writing T = 25 °C inside PV = nRT is one of the most common exam mistakes.
sections.why: These three laws combine into the ideal-gas equation you will use constantly in stoichiometry and lab calculations.

sections.heading: The ideal-gas equation
paragraphs: Ideal-gas law: PV = nRT. P is pressure, V volume, n amount in moles, T temperature in kelvin, and R the gas constant.

Match R to your units. Common choice: R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when P is in atm and V is in liters. Another: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ = 8.314 Pa·m³·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. If P is in torr, convert to atm first (760 torr = 1 atm) or use a matching R.
Rearrangements: P = nRT/V, V = nRT/P, n = PV/RT, T = PV/nR. Always write units in the setup so they cancel.
Unit trap: if V is in mL, convert to L before using R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. If P is in torr, divide by 760 to get atm.
Another common R: 62.36 L·torr·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ if you keep P in torr and V in L. Pick one system and stay inside it.
You can solve for any one variable if the other three are known. Highlight the unknown, write the rearranged equation, substitute with units, then compute.
Sig figs: temperatures like 25 °C → 298 K already limit precision; do not report ten digits from the calculator.
Quick check after a P calculation: if you have about 1 mol in about 25 L at room temperature, P should be near 1 atm. If your answer is 50 atm or 0.01 atm, reread the numbers.

worked.title: Pressure of 2.50 mol gas in 10.0 L at 25.0 °C
steps: Convert temperature: T = 25.0 + 273.15 = 298.15 K.
Choose R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ because V is in L and we want P in atm.
Write P = nRT / V.
Substitute: P = (2.50 mol)(0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹)(298.15 K) / (10.0 L).
Sig figs: 2.50, 10.0, and 25.0 support 3 sig figs.
Final answer: 6.12 atm.

workedExamples.title: Volume of 0.500 mol O₂ at 1.00 atm and 273 K
steps: This matches the molar volume 22.4 L/mol times 0.500 mol.
Final answer: 11.2 L.

sections.heading: Molar mass and density
paragraphs: From PV = nRT and n = m/M (mass over molar mass), you get PM = dRT, or d = PM/RT, where d is mass density (m/V). At fixed T and P, density is proportional to molar mass.
That is why CO₂ (44.01 g/mol) is denser than N₂ (28.02 g/mol) in the same room conditions, and why a CO₂ fire extinguisher can push oxygen away near the floor.
You can also find an unknown molar mass: measure m, V, P, T for a gas sample, then M = mRT / PV.
At the same T and P, the denser ideal gas always has the larger molar mass. Ranking densities is then just ranking M values.
For air ≈ 29 g/mol, any gas with M > 29 tends to sink in air (same T,P), and M < 29 tends to rise, ignoring drafts and temperature differences.
Experimental molar mass of a volatile liquid: weigh a flask, add liquid, heat to vaporize and fill the flask with vapor at known T and P, then reweigh. M = mRT/PV.
Watch density units. g/L is common from this equation with R = 0.082057. If a problem wants g/mL, divide by 1000.

worked.title: Density of CO₂ at 1.00 atm and 298 K
steps: Use d = PM / RT with R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.
d = (1.00 atm)(44.01 g/mol) / [(0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹)(298 K)].
Final answer: 1.80 g/L (3 sig figs).

workedExamples.title: Molar mass from 0.882 g occupying 0.500 L at 1.00 atm and 300. K
steps: M = mRT / PV.
Divide by 0.500: M = 43.4 g/mol.
Final answer: 43.4 g/mol.

sections.heading: Dalton's law of partial pressures
paragraphs: In a mixture of ideal gases, each gas behaves as if it alone occupied the volume. Dalton's law: P<sub>total</sub> = P₁ + P₂ + … = Σ P<sub>i</sub>.
Mole fraction of gas i: x<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub> / n<sub>total</sub>. Then P<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>total</sub>. Also x<sub>i</sub> = P<sub>i</sub> / P<sub>total</sub>.
Collecting a gas over water: the total pressure includes water vapor. P<sub>gas</sub> = P<sub>total</sub> − P<sub>H</sub>₂O (look up vapor pressure of water at that temperature).
Mole fractions in a mixture always sum to 1. Partial pressures always sum to P<sub>total</sub>. Those two checks catch many arithmetic errors.
When a problem gives volume percents of gases mixed at the same T and P, volume percent equals mole percent for ideal gases.
Dry gas means you already subtracted water vapor. Wet gas means P<sub>total</sub> includes P<sub>H</sub>₂O.
Example: H₂ collected over water at 25 °C with barometer 758 torr. P<sub>H</sub>₂O ≈ 23.8 torr at 25 °C. Then P<sub>H</sub>₂ = 758 − 23.8 = 734.2 torr.

worked.title: Partial pressure of O₂
steps: Given: n(N₂) = 0.400 mol, n(O₂) = 0.100 mol, P<sub>total</sub> = 2.00 atm.
P(O₂) = x(O₂) × P<sub>total</sub> = 0.200 × 2.00 atm = 0.400 atm.
Final answer: 0.400 atm.

mistake.wrong: Using Celsius temperature directly in PV = nRT (for example plugging T = 25 instead of 298).
mistake.whyWrong: Gas laws are proportional to absolute temperature. Using 25 in place of 298 understates T by a factor of about 12 and wrecks P or V.
mistake.correct: Always convert to kelvin first: T = t(°C) + 273.15.

sections.heading: Gases in reaction stoichiometry
paragraphs: Combine a balanced equation with PV = nRT. A common path: find moles of a gas from P, V, T → use mole ratios → convert the other substance to grams or to a new gas volume.
At the same T and P, gas volume ratios equal mole ratios for ideal gases. That lets you skip an intermediate mole calculation when every species of interest is a gas under the same conditions.
If both product and reactant are gases at the same T and P, volumes follow coefficients directly. Example: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ means 1 L N₂ reacts with 3 L H₂ to make 2 L NH₃ (ideal, same T,P).
If conditions differ, convert each gas to moles with PV = nRT before applying the mole ratio.
Limiting reactant still applies. Convert every reactant to moles (using PV = nRT for gases), then see which reactant runs out first from the mole ratios.
Report gas volumes only at the T and P stated. "Liters of O₂" without conditions is incomplete.
Mass–volume bridge: grams → moles (molar mass) → mole ratio → moles of gas → volume from PV = nRT. Keep a clear chain so units cancel at each step.

worked.title: Volume of O₂ at 1.00 atm and 298 K from 2.00 g KClO₃ (2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂)
steps: Moles KClO₃ = 2.00 g / 122.55 g/mol = 0.01632 mol.
Mole ratio: 3 mol O₂ / 2 mol KClO₃.
Sig figs from 2.00 g → 3 sig figs: 0.599 L.
Final answer: 0.599 L O₂.

sections.heading: Kinetic-molecular theory
paragraphs: Kinetic-molecular theory (KMT) models an ideal gas as many tiny particles in constant random motion. Postulates in plain words:
1. Particle volume is negligible compared with the container volume.
2. Particles move in straight lines until they collide.
3. Collisions with walls and with each other are elastic (no net loss of kinetic energy).
4. Attractions and repulsions between particles are negligible.
5. The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the absolute temperature.
Pressure is the result of collisions with the walls. Faster or more frequent hits raise the pressure.

Temperature measures average translational kinetic energy. At absolute zero the average KE would be zero in this classical picture (real quantum systems still have zero-point energy, which intro KMT ignores).

Collisions with the wall transfer momentum. More moles in the same volume → more collisions → higher pressure. Higher T → faster molecules → harder hits → higher pressure. That is Boyle and Amontons/Gay-Lussac in molecular language.
Ideal gas means the KMT assumptions hold well enough for PV = nRT to be accurate. Real gases are closest to ideal when dilute and warm.
Elastic collisions keep the total kinetic energy of the particles constant in a closed insulated box. Temperature stays steady when no energy leaves the system.
Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions. Lower pressure → longer mean free path. That is why effusion and vacuum systems need low pressure to work cleanly.

From wall collisions you can derive that P = (1/3) ρ u<sub>rms</sub>² for an ideal gas, where ρ is mass density. Combine that with KE<sub>avg</sub> = (3/2) RT and you recover PV = nRT. So the ideal-gas law is not a separate mystery; it follows from the postulates.
sections.why: KMT explains why PV = nRT works, and it points to the places real gases fail: finite size and attractions.

sections.heading: Molecular speed and kinetic energy
paragraphs: Average translational kinetic energy per mole of gas is (3/2) RT, with R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. Per molecule it is (3/2) kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant.
Root-mean-square speed: u<sub>rms</sub> = √(3RT / M). Here M must be in kg/mol so that the units under the square root become m²/s². Example: N₂ is 28.02 g/mol = 0.02802 kg/mol.
At the same T, lighter molecules have higher u<sub>rms</sub>. H₂ is much faster than O₂ at room temperature. Raising T raises every gas's u<sub>rms</sub>.

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution spreads molecular speeds. u<sub>rms</sub> is one characteristic speed; the most probable speed and the average speed are slightly smaller. Intro problems usually ask for u<sub>rms</sub>.
Because KE<sub>avg</sub> depends only on T, not on M, two gases at the same T have the same average KE per mole, even if their u<sub>rms</sub> values differ.
Unit trap for u<sub>rms</sub>: molar mass must be kg/mol when R is in J. Using 28.02 g/mol without converting gives an answer too large by √1000.
Heavier gases move slower at the same T, but each mole still carries (3/2)RT of translational KE. The energy is the same; the speed is not.

Example scale: at 300 K, u<sub>rms</sub>(H₂) is about 1.9 km/s, u<sub>rms</sub>(N₂) about 0.52 km/s, and u<sub>rms</sub>(CO₂) a bit lower still. Molecules are fast; macroscopic diffusion looks slow only because of constant collisions.
If T doubles, KE<sub>avg</sub> doubles and u<sub>rms</sub> rises by √2 ≈ 1.41. If M quadruples at fixed T, u<sub>rms</sub> falls by half. Those two scalings cover most qualitative speed questions.

worked.title: u<sub>rms</sub> of N₂ at 300. K
steps: Molar mass M = 28.02 g/mol = 0.02802 kg/mol.
R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. Note 1 J = 1 kg·m²·s⁻².
Write u<sub>rms</sub> = √(3RT / M).
Square root: √267045 = 516.8 m/s.
Sig figs: 300. K has 3 sig figs → 517 m/s.
Final answer: 517 m/s.

workedExamples.title: Compare u<sub>rms</sub> of H₂ and O₂ at the same T
steps: u<sub>rms</sub> ∝ 1/√M at fixed T.
u<sub>rms</sub>(H₂)/u<sub>rms</sub>(O₂) = √(M<sub>O</sub>₂ / M<sub>H</sub>₂) = √(32.00 / 2.016) = √15.87 = 3.98.
H₂ molecules move about 3.98 times faster than O₂ molecules at the same temperature.
Final answer: ratio ≈ 3.98.

sections.heading: Effusion and Graham's law
paragraphs: Effusion is escape of gas through a tiny hole into vacuum. Diffusion is mixing of gases through each other.
Graham's law: rate of effusion ∝ 1/√M. For two gases at the same T and P: rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁). The lighter gas effuses faster.
The same square-root mass dependence appears in u<sub>rms</sub>, because faster molecules hit the hole more often.
Time to effuse is inversely related to rate. If gas A effuses twice as fast as gas B, A needs half the time to pass the same amount through the hole.
Enrichment of uranium used gaseous UF₆ effusion historically: lighter ²³⁵UF₆ effuses slightly faster than ²³⁸UF₆. The mass difference is small, so many stages were needed.

Graham's law also estimates diffusion rates in free space when other factors are similar. In air, perfume molecules still meet air molecules, so real diffusion is slower than simple effusion through a pinhole.
If a problem gives times instead of rates, remember t ∝ 1/rate ∝ √M. The gas with larger M takes longer.

Worked pattern: write the ratio with the unknown rate or time on the left, put molar masses under square roots on the right, then solve. Cancel identical T and P assumptions that Graham's law already requires.
Sample trap: mixing up which mass goes on top. Always put the other gas's molar mass under the square root when you want rate<sub>A</sub> / rate<sub>B</sub> = √(M<sub>B</sub> / M<sub>A</sub>).

worked.title: H₂ vs O₂ effusion rate ratio
steps: M(H₂) = 2.016 g/mol. M(O₂) = 32.00 g/mol.
rate(H₂)/rate(O₂) = √(M<sub>O</sub>₂ / M<sub>H</sub>₂) = √(32.00 / 2.016).
Final answer: H₂ effuses about 3.98 times as fast as O₂.

workedExamples.title: Which effuses faster, CH₄ or He? By what factor?
steps: M(He) = 4.003 g/mol. M(CH₄) = 16.04 g/mol.
He is lighter → He effuses faster.
Final answer: He effuses about 2.00 times as fast as CH₄.

mistake.wrong: Writing rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₁/M₂) and concluding the heavier gas is faster.
mistake.whyWrong: The lighter gas is faster. The molar mass of the other gas goes under the square root in the numerator.
mistake.correct: Use rate<sub>light</sub> / rate<sub>heavy</sub> = √(M<sub>heavy</sub> / M<sub>light</sub>).

sections.heading: Real gases and van der Waals
paragraphs: Real gases approach ideal behavior at low pressure and high temperature: particles are far apart, so their size and attractions matter less.
Deviations grow at high pressure (particle volume is no longer negligible) and at low temperature (attractions particles stick together more).

van der Waals equation: (P + a n²/V²)(V − n b) = nRT. The a term corrects for attractions (attractions reduce the force of wall collisions, so you add a pressure correction). The b term corrects for finite particle volume (available volume is V − nb).
Larger, more polarizable molecules usually have larger a. Larger molecules usually have larger b.
Compressibility factor Z = PV<sub>m</sub> / RT. For an ideal gas Z = 1. Z < 1 often signals attractions dominating; Z > 1 at high P often signals finite volume dominating.

van der Waals constants a and b are substance-specific. You look them up; you do not invent them. Problems that give a and b expect you to plug into (P + a n²/V²)(V − n b) = nRT carefully with matching units.
At very high pressure, molecules are forced close together. The excluded volume nb is a large fraction of V, so the ideal law overestimates how much you can compress the gas.
Near condensation, attractions pull molecules together and can make the observed pressure much lower than ideal. That is where Z dips below 1.

Practical rule: for many intro problems at ~1 atm and ~300 K, treat common gases as ideal unless the question names van der Waals or asks about deviations. Save a and b for the problems that give them.

Comparing gases: CO₂ has a larger a than H₂ because CO₂ is more polarizable and feels stronger attractions. CO₂ also has a larger b because the molecule is bigger. Tables of a and b make that comparison quantitative.

worked.title: When is the ideal-gas law safest?
steps: List conditions: low pressure (for example well below 1 atm, or at least not tens of atm) and temperature well above the boiling point.
Under those conditions, V is large compared with nb, and a n²/V² is small compared with P.
Then (P + small)(V − small) ≈ PV ≈ nRT.
Final answer: low P and high T (relative to the substance's condensation conditions).

workedExamples.title: Qualitative: effect of attractions on measured P
steps: Attractions pull molecules back as they approach the wall.
They hit the wall with less momentum than an ideal gas would.
Observed pressure is lower than the ideal PV = nRT prediction at the same n, V, T.
That is why the van der Waals form adds +a n²/V² inside the pressure factor: you restore the "missing" pressure in the equation.
Final answer: attractions lower observed P relative to the ideal value.

workedExamples.title: Which correction matters more as V gets very large?
steps: a n²/V² shrinks toward 0 as V grows.
n b becomes negligible compared with large V, so V − n b ≈ V.
Both corrections fade; the equation approaches PV = nRT.
Final answer: at large V (low density), both a and b corrections become unimportant.

sections.heading: First law: system, heat, and work
paragraphs: Thermochemistry tracks energy changes in chemical reactions. Define the system (the chemicals you care about) and the surroundings (everything else). Energy that leaves the system enters the surroundings.

Internal energy U is a state function: its change ΔU depends only on the start and end states, not on the path. The first law says ΔU = q + w, using the chemistry sign convention: q > 0 when heat enters the system, and w > 0 when work is done on the system.

For expansion work against a constant external pressure, w = −P<sub>ext</sub> ΔV. When a gas expands (ΔV > 0), the system does work on the surroundings, so w is negative and U falls if heat is not supplied.
Heat and work are path functions. Different routes between the same two states can exchange different amounts of heat and work, but ΔU is the same.
At constant volume, no expansion work is done (ΔV = 0), so w = 0 and ΔU = q<sub>V</sub>. Bomb calorimeters use that idea.

Open vs closed vs isolated: a closed system exchanges energy but not matter; an isolated system exchanges neither. Coffee-cup calorimeters are approximately adiabatic toward the room for a short experiment, but they are open to constant pressure.
Electrical work and other forms exist, but intro problems focus on heat and PV work. Keep the sign convention consistent with your course: here q and w into the system are positive.
Common state functions: U, H, S, G, P, T, V. Path functions for energy transfer: q and w. Exam questions often ask which quantities depend only on the current state.
sections.why: Every enthalpy and calorimetry problem sits on ΔU = q + w and on clear system/surroundings bookkeeping.

worked.title: Sign of q and w for a gas that expands while absorbing heat
steps: The gas (system) expands → ΔV > 0 → w = −P<sub>ext</sub> ΔV < 0 (system does work).
The gas absorbs heat → q > 0.
ΔU = q + w could be positive, negative, or zero depending on which term is larger.
Final answer: q positive, w negative; ΔU needs the magnitudes.

workedExamples.title: ΔU when q = +150 J and w = −40 J
steps: The system gained 110 J of internal energy.
Final answer: ΔU = +110 J.

sections.heading: Enthalpy and calorimetry
paragraphs: Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV. It is also a state function. At constant pressure, the heat transferred equals the enthalpy change: q<sub>p</sub> = ΔH.
Most open-lab reactions run at (nearly) constant atmospheric pressure, so tabulated reaction heats are usually ΔH values.

Coffee-cup (constant-pressure) calorimetry: the solution absorbs or releases heat. For a dilute aqueous reaction, qsol ≈ m c ΔT, where m is the mass of solution, c is the specific heat capacity (often ≈ 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹ for dilute water solutions), and ΔT = Tfinal − Tinitial.

Energy conservation: heat gained by the solution equals heat lost by the reaction (or the reverse). So q<sub>rxn</sub> = −q<sub>sol</sub> for an insulated cup that only exchanges heat between reaction and solution.
If the reaction is exothermic, the solution warms (ΔT > 0), q<sub>sol</sub> > 0, and q<sub>rxn</sub> < 0, so ΔH < 0. Endothermic reactions cool the solution.
To report ΔH per mole, divide q<sub>rxn</sub> by the moles of the limiting reactant that reacted (watch the sign).
Bomb (constant-volume) calorimetry measures q<sub>V</sub> ≈ ΔU for the combustion. Converting to ΔH needs the Δn<sub>g</sub> RT correction when asked.
Specific heat capacity c is per gram; molar heat capacity C is per mole. Do not mix them. Watch whether ΔT is in °C or K. The size of the degree is the same, so ΔT values match.

If two solutions are mixed, m is usually the total mass after mixing. If volumes add and density is about 1.00 g/mL, total mass in grams matches total volume in mL. That shortcut appears in many coffee-cup problems.
Limiting reactant still controls q<sub>rxn</sub> when one reagent runs out. Convert q<sub>rxn</sub> to ΔH per mole using moles reacted, not moles originally present of the excess reagent.

worked.title: ΔH from coffee-cup data
steps: Given: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl mixes with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH. Solution mass ≈ 100.0 g (density ≈ 1.00 g/mL). c = 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹. Temperature rises 6.50 °C.
qsol = m c ΔT = (100.0 g)(4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)(6.50 °C) = 2717 J = 2.717 kJ.
q<sub>rxn</sub> = −q<sub>sol</sub> = −2.717 kJ.
Moles of water formed: HCl and NaOH are 1:1; moles = 0.0500 L × 1.00 mol/L = 0.0500 mol.
ΔH per mole = q<sub>rxn</sub> / n = −2.717 kJ / 0.0500 mol = −54.3 kJ/mol.
Sign check: temperature rose → exothermic → negative ΔH. Good.
Final answer: ΔH ≈ −54.3 kJ per mole of reaction as written for 1 mol H₂O.

workedExamples.title: qsol when 75.0 g water cools by 3.20 °C (c = 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)
steps: ΔT = −3.20 °C (cooling).
The water lost heat. If this cooling came from an endothermic reaction in the cup, q<sub>rxn</sub> = −q<sub>sol</sub> = +1.00 × 10³ J.
Final answer: q<sub>sol</sub> = −1.00 × 10³ J.

sections.heading: Hess's law and standard enthalpies of formation
paragraphs: Hess's law: if a reaction is the sum of steps, ΔH for the reaction is the sum of the ΔH values of the steps. Enthalpy is a state function, so the path does not matter.

Standard enthalpy of formation ΔH<sub>f</sub>° is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance forms from its elements in their standard states. By definition, ΔH<sub>f</sub>° = 0 for an element in its standard state (O₂(g), C(graphite), H₂(g), …).
For any reaction: ΔH<sub>rxn</sub>° = Σ n ΔH<sub>f</sub>°(products) − Σ n ΔH<sub>f</sub>°(reactants), with stoichiometric coefficients n.
Always match physical states to the table (H₂O(l) vs H₂O(g) differ by the enthalpy of vaporization).
Hess's law is also how you combine measured combustion or formation reactions when a direct measurement is hard.
Standard state means the pure substance at 1 bar (older tables: 1 atm) and the specified temperature, usually 298 K for tables labeled °.
If a problem gives ΔH for a reaction written with fractional coefficients, you may scale everything, including ΔH, by the same factor to match integer moles.

Formation enthalpies can be positive (endothermic formation, as for NO) or negative (exothermic formation, as for CO₂ and H₂O). A positive ΔH<sub>f</sub>° does not mean the compound cannot exist; it means forming it from elements absorbs heat.
Think of a formation cycle: elements → compounds with tabulated ΔH<sub>f</sub>°, then rearrange. Hess's law is that cycle written as algebra.
sections.why: Tables of ΔH<sub>f</sub>° turn many exam ΔH questions into careful arithmetic with correct signs and states.

worked.title: ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l)
steps: Use ΔH<sub>f</sub>° values (kJ/mol): CH₄(g) = −74.8, O₂(g) = 0, CO₂(g) = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8.
Sign check: combustion is exothermic → negative. Good.
Final answer: ΔH° ≈ −890.3 kJ.

workedExamples.title: Hess path: find ΔH for C(graphite) + ½ O₂ → CO when given combustion data
steps: Given: C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₁ = −393.5 kJ; CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₂ = −283.0 kJ.
Target: C + ½ O₂ → CO.
Take reaction 1 as written. Reverse reaction 2 (flip sign): CO₂ → CO + ½ O₂, ΔH = +283.0 kJ.
Add: C + O₂ + CO₂ → CO₂ + CO + ½ O₂. Cancel CO₂ and cancel ½ O₂ from each side.
Left with C + ½ O₂ → CO. ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ.
Final answer: ΔH = −110.5 kJ.

mistake.wrong: Forgetting to flip the sign when a formation reaction is reversed, or mixing H₂O(l) and H₂O(g) values.
mistake.whyWrong: Hess's law and ΔH<sub>f</sub>° arithmetic both depend on matching the exact reaction as written. A reversed step needs −ΔH. Wrong state uses the wrong table entry.
mistake.correct: Write the target equation, line up each step or each ΔH<sub>f</sub>° with its state, flip signs when you reverse, then subtract Σ reactants from Σ products.

sections.heading: Relating ΔH and ΔU for gas reactions
paragraphs: From H = U + PV, for ideal-gas reactions at constant T: ΔH ≈ ΔU + Δn<sub>g</sub> RT, where Δn<sub>g</sub> is moles of gas products minus moles of gas reactants (from the balanced equation).
R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. Keep ΔH and ΔU in the same energy unit (often convert RT into kJ).
If Δn<sub>g</sub> = 0 (same gas moles on both sides), ΔH ≈ ΔU. If gas moles increase, ΔH is more positive than ΔU by about Δn<sub>g</sub> RT.
Only gas moles enter Δn<sub>g</sub>. Solids and liquids are omitted from that count because their molar volumes are tiny compared with gases.
Example check: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g) has Δn<sub>g</sub> = 0, so ΔH ≈ ΔU.

worked.title: ΔU from ΔH for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g) at 298 K if ΔH = −92.2 kJ
steps: Δn<sub>g</sub> = 2 − (1 + 3) = 2 − 4 = −2 mol gas.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn<sub>g</sub> RT ⇒ ΔU = ΔH − Δn<sub>g</sub> RT.
RT = (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹)(298 K) = 2.478 kJ/mol.
Final answer: ΔU ≈ −87.2 kJ for the reaction as written.

sections.heading: Equilibrium constants K and Q
paragraphs: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stop changing.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant in concentration form is K<sub>c</sub> = ([C]<sup>c</sup> [D]<sup>d</sup>) / ([A]<sup>a</sup> [B]<sup>b</sup>), using equilibrium concentrations. Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in K.

The reaction quotient Q uses the same algebraic form with current (not necessarily equilibrium) values. Compare Q with K: if Q < K, the forward reaction is favored until equilibrium; if Q > K, the reverse; if Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.

Kp uses partial pressures (often in bar, or atm when that matches the standard used in the problem). For ideal gases, Kp = Kc (RT)Δn where Δn = (c + d) − (a + b) counting gas moles only, and R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when pressures are in atm and concentrations in mol/L.
K depends only on temperature for a given reaction. Catalysts and the amounts you mix change how fast you get there or the position along the path, but they do not change K itself at fixed T.

Writing K: products over reactants, each concentration or pressure raised to its coefficient. Never put solid CaCO₃ or liquid H₂O into K<sub>c</sub> for heterogeneous equilibria like CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g); there K<sub>p</sub> = P<sub>CO</sub>₂.
Large K means products dominate at equilibrium. Small K means reactants dominate. K = 1 means a balanced mix under the standard-state convention.
Numerical values of K depend on how the equation is written. Double every coefficient and you square K. Reverse the equation and K becomes 1/K. Always match K to the equation on the page.
Partial pressures in K<sub>p</sub> must use the same pressure unit the tabulated K<sub>p</sub> assumes. Mixing bar and atm without converting creates silent errors.
Q uses the same formula as K but with the concentrations or pressures you have right now. Updating one species changes Q instantly; K stays put until temperature changes.
When all stoichiometric coefficients are multiplied by a factor n, the new constant is the old constant raised to n. That rule keeps thermodynamics consistent with how the equation is written.
That one comparison prevents most guesswork.
sections.why: Q vs K is the fastest way to predict direction before you solve an ICE table.

worked.title: Direction from Q for N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃
steps: Suppose K<sub>c</sub> = 0.0602 and current concentrations are [N₂] = 0.50, [H₂] = 0.50, [NH₃] = 0.50 (all mol/L).
Q<sub>c</sub> = 4.0 > K<sub>c</sub> = 0.0602 → too many products relative to equilibrium.
Net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction (NH₃ decomposes) until Q falls to K.
Final answer: reverse direction.

workedExamples.title: Convert K<sub>c</sub> to K<sub>p</sub> for N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃ at 400. K
steps: K<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>c</sub> (RT)<sup>Δn</sup> = K<sub>c</sub> (RT)<sup>−2</sup> = K<sub>c</sub> / (RT)².
Final answer: K<sub>p</sub> ≈ 4.64 × 10⁻⁴.

sections.heading: ICE tables
paragraphs: An ICE table organizes Initial concentrations (or moles in a known volume), the Change in terms of x using stoichiometry, and Equilibrium values as Initial + Change.
Substitute the equilibrium row into the K expression and solve for x. Then back-substitute to get each equilibrium concentration.

Approximation: if K is small and the initial reactant concentration C is not tiny, x ≈ √(K × something) may be ≪ C. Check that x/C < about 0.05 (5% rule) before you trust the approximation; otherwise solve the exact quadratic.
Units: keep a consistent concentration unit (usually mol/L). For K<sub>p</sub> problems, use partial pressures in the unit your K<sub>p</sub> expects.

When the stoichiometry is 1:1:1 with a moderate K, you often get a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0. Use x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / (2a) and keep the root that makes physical sense (concentrations ≥ 0).
Starting from pure products is fine: then x measures reverse change. Always define x clearly in the Change row.
Common pattern: start with reactants only, define +x on the product side using the stoichiometric ratios, substitute into K, solve, then report all equilibrium concentrations with correct sig figs.
If a problem gives K<sub>p</sub> and pressures, build the ICE table in partial pressures (or convert everything to moles in a known volume first). Do not mix [ ] and P in one expression.
Sanity check after solving: plug equilibrium values back into the K expression and confirm you recover the given K within rounding error.
When K is very large, equilibrium lies far to the right. Sometimes it is easier to push the reaction to completion first, then define x as a small reverse change.

worked.title: ICE for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) with K<sub>c</sub> = 50.0
steps: Start with [H₂]₀ = 1.00 M, [I₂]₀ = 1.00 M, [HI]₀ = 0.
Change: H₂ and I₂ each −x; HI +2x.
Equilibrium: [H₂] = 1.00 − x, [I₂] = 1.00 − x, [HI] = 2x.
Take square root: 2x / (1 − x) = √50.0 = 7.071.
Final answer: [HI] = 1.56 M; [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.220 M.

workedExamples.title: Small-K approximation for A ⇌ B + C with K<sub>c</sub> = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶, [A]₀ = 0.20 M
steps: Equilibrium: [A] = 0.20 − x, [B] = [C] = x.
Check: x / 0.20 = 0.0032 (0.32%) ≪ 5% → approximation OK.
Final answer: [B] = [C] = 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ M.

mistake.wrong: Putting stoichiometric coefficients into the exponents of K incorrectly, or treating solids as if they belong in K<sub>c</sub>.
mistake.whyWrong: K uses equilibrium activities. Pure solids and liquids are omitted. Coefficients become exponents on the species that do appear, not multipliers in front of K.
mistake.correct: Write K only with gases and solutes, each raised to its coefficient. Drop pure solids and liquids.

sections.heading: Le Châtelier's principle
paragraphs: Le Châtelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, the net reaction shifts to partially counteract the disturbance.
Add reactant → forward shift. Add product → reverse shift. Remove a product → forward shift.

Increase pressure by decreasing volume → shift toward fewer gas moles. Decrease pressure → toward more gas moles. Adding inert gas at constant volume does not change partial pressures of reactants/products the same way; for ideal gases at constant V, K<sub>p</sub> problems often show no shift.

Temperature: treat heat as a reactant in an endothermic reaction or as a product in an exothermic one. Raising T shifts toward the endothermic direction and changes K (K increases with T for endothermic reactions).
A catalyst speeds both directions equally. It shortens the time to equilibrium but does not change K or the equilibrium position.
Concentration stresses change Q immediately; the system then shifts until Q returns to K. Temperature stresses change K itself.
Adding a solid reactant does not change its activity (still 1), so it does not shift a heterogeneous equilibrium the way adding a solute would.
Industrial ammonia (Haber) uses moderate T (kinetics vs equilibrium tradeoff), high P (favors NH₃), and continuous product removal. That is Le Châtelier in engineering form.
Removing heat (cooling an exothermic equilibrium) favors products. That is why some industrial reactors cool the mixture after reaction to lock in conversion, combined with kinetics considerations.

Volume and pressure stresses matter only when Δn<sub>gas</sub> ≠ 0. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI, gas moles stay 2 = 2, so compression does not shift the position (K<sub>x</sub> unchanged for that stoichiometry).

Exam wording trap: "the equilibrium shifts left" means the reverse net reaction makes more reactants until Q returns to K. Concentrations of products fall; concentrations of reactants rise (for a closed system without removal).

worked.title: Shift for 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 SO₃(g) (exothermic) when T rises
steps: Exothermic means heat is on the product side in the Le Châtelier picture.
Raising T is like adding heat → reverse shift (toward SO₂ and O₂).
K decreases because the reverse direction is favored at the new equilibrium.
Final answer: reverse shift; K smaller.

workedExamples.title: Effect of compressing N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃
steps: Gas moles: left 4, right 2.
Compressing (higher P, smaller V) favors fewer gas moles → forward (more NH₃).
Final answer: forward shift toward NH₃.

workedExamples.title: Add inert gas at constant pressure to N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃
steps: At constant P, adding inert gas increases total volume.
Partial pressures of N₂, H₂, and NH₃ fall (mole fractions drop).
Lower partial pressures of N₂, H₂, and NH₃ act like a pressure drop → shift toward more gas moles → reverse.
Final answer: reverse shift (at constant P).

sections.heading: Entropy and predicting ΔS
paragraphs: Entropy S measures how widely energy and matter are dispersed. More microstates → higher entropy. It is a state function.
Typical order for a pure substance: S(gas) ≫ S(liquid) > S(solid). Dissolving a solid or liquid in a solvent usually increases entropy; dissolving a gas in a liquid usually decreases entropy.

For a chemical reaction, count gas moles first: if moles of gas increase, ΔS° is often positive; if they decrease, ΔS° is often negative. Phase changes and complexity matter too, but gas count is the best first check.
Third-law entropies: tables list standard molar entropies S° (not ΔS<sub>f</sub>°). Elements do not have S° = 0 (except a perfect crystal at 0 K).
ΔS<sub>rxn</sub>° = Σ n S°(products) − Σ n S°(reactants).
Second law: for any spontaneous process, the total entropy of the system plus surroundings increases: ΔS<sub>univ</sub> = ΔS<sub>sys</sub> + ΔS<sub>surr</sub> > 0.

At constant T and P, heat into the surroundings relates to −ΔH<sub>sys</sub> / T for the surroundings when the only exchange is that heat, so ΔS<sub>surr</sub> ≈ −ΔH<sub>sys</sub> / T. That is why exothermic reactions can drive ΔS<sub>univ</sub> up even if ΔS<sub>sys</sub> is negative.
Absolute entropy rises with temperature and with molecular complexity (more ways to store energy). Ne(g) has lower S° than C₂H₆(g) at the same T.
Entropy is not "disorder" in a casual desk-mess sense. It is a count of how many microscopic arrangements match the same macroscopic state. Still, the gas-vs-solid intuition is a useful ranking tool.

For the surroundings at constant T, an exothermic system (ΔH<sub>sys</sub> < 0) dumps heat that increases S<sub>surr</sub>. That is why many exothermic reactions with negative ΔS<sub>sys</sub> are still spontaneous at low T.

Heating a substance slowly and reversibly adds entropy ΔS = q<sub>rev</sub> / T. For a constant-pressure warm-up without phase change, that becomes integral of C<sub>p</sub> dT / T, which is why larger heat capacity means a larger entropy increase for the same temperature jump.
Mixing two ideal gases increases entropy because the number of position microstates rises. That is a standard ΔS > 0 example with no chemistry at all.
Quick ranking drill: compare moles of gas first, then phases, then molecular complexity. That order of checks solves most qualitative ΔS questions on exams.

Tabulated S° values already include all the heating and phase-change entropy from 0 K up to 298 K for the standard state. That is why you can subtract Σ S°(reactants) from Σ S°(products) without inventing extra terms for "starting from elements."
sections.why: Sign of ΔS, together with ΔH, decides how temperature affects spontaneity through ΔG.

worked.title: Sign of ΔS for 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l)
steps: Gas moles left: 3. Gas moles right: 0 (liquid water).
Gases disappear into a liquid → much less dispersal.
ΔS° is negative (and large in magnitude).
Final answer: ΔS° < 0.

workedExamples.title: ΔS° for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g) from table values
steps: Suppose S° (J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹): N₂ = 191.6, H₂ = 130.7, NH₃ = 192.8.
Matches fewer gas moles (4 → 2).
Final answer: ΔS° ≈ −198.1 J/K.

workedExamples.title: Predict ΔS sign: dissolving NaCl(s) in water
steps: Solid ions become mobile hydrated ions in solution.
Number of accessible microstates rises.
ΔS<sub>sys</sub> is positive for dissolving NaCl.
Final answer: ΔS > 0.

sections.heading: Gibbs energy and spontaneity
paragraphs: Gibbs free energy G combines enthalpy and entropy for processes at constant T and P. The change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with T in kelvin.
At constant T and P: ΔG < 0 means the process is spontaneous as written; ΔG > 0 means the reverse is spontaneous; ΔG = 0 means equilibrium.

Standard change ΔG° uses standard states. Signs of ΔH° and ΔS° create four cases: both negative → spontaneous at low T; both positive → spontaneous at high T; ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0 → always spontaneous; ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° < 0 → never spontaneous (as written under standard conditions).
The crossover temperature where ΔG° = 0 is T = ΔH° / ΔS° (use consistent units; convert J and kJ carefully).
ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work available from a process at constant T and P (a useful interpretation, even when you only use the sign).
Standard vs nonstandard: tables give ΔG°, ΔH°, S°. Real mixtures use ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. Spontaneity under lab conditions depends on ΔG, not only ΔG°.
Phase changes at the normal boiling or melting point are at equilibrium: ΔG = 0 and ΔH = TΔS for the reversible phase change.

Plotting ΔG vs T as a straight line with slope −ΔS (when ΔH and ΔS are taken as constant) shows when the line crosses zero. That crossing is the temperature where reactants and products are balanced under standard conditions.
Biological and materials problems often ask whether a process is enthalpy-driven or entropy-driven. Look at which term dominates ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
Spontaneous does not mean fast. Diamond converting to graphite has ΔG < 0 at room temperature, yet the rate is negligible. Kinetics and thermodynamics answer different questions.
When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature is the switch. Learn the four-case table until you can rebuild it without notes.

Units drill: if ΔH° = −85.0 kJ and ΔS° = −150. J/K at 298 K, convert ΔS° to −0.150 kJ/K, then TΔS° = −44.7 kJ, so ΔG° = −85.0 − (−44.7) = −40.3 kJ. Missing the joule conversion would wreck the sign logic.

Coupled processes: a nonspontaneous step can be pulled forward when it is linked to a highly spontaneous step (as in many biochemical pathways). The sum of ΔG values for the coupled path must be negative.

worked.title: Is a reaction spontaneous at 298 K if ΔH° = +40.0 kJ and ΔS° = +150. J/K?
steps: Convert: ΔS° = 0.150 kJ/K.
ΔG° < 0 → spontaneous under standard conditions at 298 K.
Final answer: yes; ΔG° ≈ −4.7 kJ.

workedExamples.title: Find T where ΔG° = 0 for ΔH° = +40.0 kJ, ΔS° = +150. J/K
steps: Above 267 K, −TΔS outweighs +ΔH → ΔG° < 0.
Final answer: about 267 K.

workedExamples.title: Classify spontaneity: ΔH° < 0, ΔS° > 0
steps: ΔH° negative favors ΔG° < 0.
−TΔS° is also negative when ΔS° > 0.
Both terms drive ΔG° down at every T.
Final answer: spontaneous at all temperatures (under standard conditions).

mistake.wrong: Mixing joules and kilojoules in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (for example subtracting 298 × 150 from 40).
mistake.whyWrong: ΔH is often in kJ while ΔS tables are in J/K. 298 × 150 = 44700 J = 44.7 kJ, not 44700 kJ. Unit mismatch flips the conclusion.
mistake.correct: Convert ΔS to kJ/K (divide by 1000) or convert ΔH to J before subtracting TΔS.

sections.heading: ΔG° and the equilibrium constant
paragraphs: Thermodynamics links to equilibrium by ΔG° = −RT ln K. If ΔG° < 0, then ln K > 0 and K > 1 (products favored at equilibrium). If ΔG° > 0, K < 1.

R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. K must be the thermodynamic equilibrium constant (dimensionless activities). In intro problems, Kc or Kp is often plugged in as an approximation when the standard states match the problem.
Away from standard conditions, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0.
Because ln K appears, a modest change in ΔG° swings K a lot. Roughly every −5.7 kJ/mol of ΔG° at 298 K multiplies K by about 10.
If a problem gives K<sub>p</sub> or K<sub>c</sub>, confirm whether the course treats that value as the K in ΔG° = −RT ln K. Many intro problems do.
When Q < K, ΔG is negative and the forward reaction is spontaneous under those conditions even if ΔG° is positive. Standard and actual conditions are different questions.
Solving for K: K = e<sup>−ΔG° / RT</sup>. Solving for ΔG°: ΔG° = −RT ln K. Keep R and ΔG° in matching energy units (J vs kJ).
A reaction can have K ≪ 1 and still make useful product if you remove product continuously (Le Châtelier), but the thermodynamic K itself stays small at that T.
Large positive ΔG° means tiny K; large negative ΔG° means huge K. You do not need a calculator to know which side equilibrium favors once you know the sign of ΔG°.

worked.title: K from ΔG° = −20.0 kJ/mol at 298 K
steps: Final answer: K ≈ 3.2 × 10³.

items.a: Increase. Liquid water has more microstates than ice.

sections.heading: Rate laws and reaction order
paragraphs: Kinetics studies how fast reactions go. Average rate over a time interval is Δ(concentration)/Δt with a sign chosen so rates are positive; use stoichiometric coefficients to relate rates of different species.

A differential rate law for aA + bB → products often looks like rate = k [A]<sup>m</sup> [B]<sup>n</sup>. The exponents m and n are orders. They are found from experiment, not from the balanced equation (unless the reaction is an elementary step).
Overall order is m + n. The rate constant k has units that depend on overall order (for example, for first order, time⁻¹; for second order, L·mol⁻¹·time⁻¹).
Method of initial rates: measure rate at t ≈ 0 for several starting concentrations. If doubling [A] doubles the rate while [B] is fixed, the reaction is first order in A.
Instantaneous rate is the slope of concentration vs time at one moment. Initial rate is the instantaneous rate at the start, before products build up or reverse reactions matter.
Rate must stay consistent with stoichiometry: for 2 N₂O₅ → 4 NO₂ + O₂, rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ is twice the rate of appearance of O₂.
Zero-order reactions still depend on having enough catalyst surface or light intensity; the rate law is zero order in the monitored concentration over a limited range.
Negative orders sometimes appear when a species inhibits the rate. Treat them as experimental facts from the data.
Rates usually fall as reactants are consumed unless a product autocatalyzes the reaction. Initial-rate methods avoid that complication by reading the beginning of each run.
Always state the rate definition you are using. Saying "the rate" without tying it to a species can be ambiguous when stoichiometric coefficients differ.
Change one concentration at a time when possible so the order in that reactant is obvious from a single pair of runs.
Concentration units inside a rate law must match how k was defined. If [A] is in mol/L and time is in seconds, first-order k is in s⁻¹ and a second-order k for rate = k[A]² is in L·mol⁻¹·s⁻¹.
sections.why: Orders tell you how concentration controls speed and which integrated law to use.

worked.title: Find orders from initial-rate data
steps: From 1→2, [A] ×2, rate ×4 → order in A is 2 (because 2² = 4).
From 1→3, [B] ×2, rate unchanged → order in B is 0.
Rate = k [A]². Using expt 1: 2.0 × 10⁻³ = k (0.10)² → k = 0.20 L·mol⁻¹·s⁻¹ (if rate is in mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹).
Final answer: second order in A, zero order in B; k = 0.20 L·mol⁻¹·s⁻¹.

workedExamples.title: Relate rates for 2 N₂O₅ → 4 NO₂ + O₂
steps: Rate = −(1/2) Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = +(1/4) Δ[NO₂]/Δt = +Δ[O₂]/Δt.
If O₂ appears at 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, N₂O₅ disappears at 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
Final answer: −Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = 2 × Δ[O₂]/Δt.

sections.heading: Integrated rate laws and half-life
paragraphs: Integrated rate laws give concentration vs time.
First order: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − k t, or [A] = [A]₀ e<sup>−kt</sup>. Plot of ln[A] vs t is linear with slope −k. Half-life t½ = ln 2 / k ≈ 0.693 / k (constant, independent of [A]₀).
Second order (rate = k[A]²): 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + k t. Half-life grows as [A]₀ falls: t½ = 1 / (k [A]₀).
Zero order: [A] = [A]₀ − k t. t½ = [A]₀ / (2k).
To identify order from data, test which plot is linear: [A] vs t (zero), ln[A] vs t (first), 1/[A] vs t (second).
Radioactive decay is first order. Carbon-14 dating uses the same integrated law with a known half-life.
Units of k are a quick order check: s⁻¹ suggests first order; M⁻¹·s⁻¹ suggests second order (for rate in M/s).
Write the integrated equation, isolate the unknown (k, t, or [A]), substitute with units, then interpret whether the answer is physical (concentration between 0 and [A]₀).
Half-life questions for first order can be solved without k: number of half-lives n = t / t½, fraction left = (1/2)<sup>n</sup>.
First-order processes appear in pharmacokinetics and environmental decay models as well as chemistry labs. The math is the same exponential decay.
If a problem gives two concentrations and the time between them for a first-order reaction, k = ln([A]₀/[A]) / t.
Second-order half-life getting longer as the reactant is consumed is a qualitative signature you can use even before plotting 1/[A].
A plot beats memorizing alone: if ln[A] vs t curves, the reaction is not first order. If 1/[A] vs t is straight, you have second order in A (for the single-reactant form).

worked.title: First-order remaining fraction after 3 half-lives
steps: Each half-life halves the amount.
After 1: 1/2. After 2: 1/4. After 3: 1/8.
Fraction left = 0.125 = 12.5%.
Final answer: 1/8 remains.

workedExamples.title: Find k if first-order t½ = 12.0 min
steps: Final answer: k = 0.0578 min⁻¹.

workedExamples.title: [A] after 10.0 min if [A]₀ = 0.800 M, first-order k = 0.0578 min⁻¹
steps: Final answer: 0.449 M.

mistake.wrong: Using t½ = 0.693/k for a second-order reaction, or reading orders from the balanced equation for a multi-step process.
mistake.whyWrong: Constant half-life is a first-order signature. Overall stoichiometry does not fix the rate law when the mechanism has more than one step.
mistake.correct: Match the integrated law to the experimental order. Use half-life formulas that belong to that order only.

sections.heading: Arrhenius equation and mechanisms
paragraphs: Most rate constants rise with temperature. The Arrhenius equation is k = A e<sup>−E<sub>a</sub> / RT</sup>, where E<sub>a</sub> is the activation energy and A is the pre-exponential factor.
Two-temperature form: ln(k₂/k₁) = −(Ea/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Temperatures in kelvin; R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.
A reaction mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps. The rate law of an elementary step follows its molecularity. The slowest step (rate-determining step) often sets the observed rate law.
Intermediates are made and consumed; they cancel in the overall reaction. Catalysts appear at the start and are regenerated; they open a path with lower E<sub>a</sub>.
Collision theory: molecules must collide with enough energy and with the right orientation. Higher T → larger fraction of collisions above E<sub>a</sub>.
A unimolecular elementary step is first order; a bimolecular elementary step is second order. Termolecular steps are rare.
If the first step is slow and the second is fast, the observed rate law often matches the first step's molecularity (when that step is elementary).
A graph of ln k vs 1/T is linear with slope −E<sub>a</sub>/R. That plot is how experimental activation energies are often extracted from several temperatures.
Activation energy is always positive for an elementary barrier in the usual picture. A larger E<sub>a</sub> means a steeper rise of k with temperature.
Homogeneous catalysts mix in the same phase; heterogeneous catalysts provide a surface. Both lower the effective barrier relative to the uncatalyzed path.
Mechanisms must sum to the overall reaction, cancel intermediates, and predict a rate law that matches experiment. If the predicted law disagrees with data, the mechanism is wrong or incomplete.
Catalysts do not appear in the overall stoichiometry as net consumers, but they can appear in the rate law if the mechanism needs them. Enzyme kinetics is the biological version of that idea.

worked.title: E<sub>a</sub> from two rate constants
steps: k₁ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at T₁ = 300. K; k₂ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at T₂ = 320. K.
Final answer: E<sub>a</sub> ≈ 55.4 kJ/mol.
Sign check: k rose when T rose, so E<sub>a</sub> must come out positive. Good.

workedExamples.title: Why a catalyst speeds a reaction without changing ΔH<sub>rxn</sub>
steps: Catalyst provides a new path with lower E<sub>a</sub>.
Lower E<sub>a</sub> → larger k at the same T → faster rates both ways.
Reactants and products (and thus ΔH between them) are unchanged; only the barrier height changes.
Final answer: lower E<sub>a</sub> on an alternate path; ΔH unchanged.

sections.heading: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases
paragraphs: Brønsted–Lowry: an acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺. After the transfer, the acid has become its conjugate base, and the base has become its conjugate acid.
Example: in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, water acts as an acid and NH₃ as a base. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃; OH⁻ is the conjugate base of H₂O.
Amphoteric species (like water or HSO₄⁻) can act as acid or base depending on the partner.
Lewis definition (broader): acid accepts an electron pair; base donates an electron pair. BF₃ + NH₃ is a Lewis acid–base example without H⁺ transfer.
Stronger acids have weaker conjugate bases. In water, strong acids donate H⁺ completely.
In any acid–base reaction, identify two conjugate pairs. The stronger acid and stronger base sit on one side; equilibrium favors the weaker acid and weaker base.
Leveling effect: in water, all strong acids look equally strong because they all convert fully to H₃O⁺.
Autoionization means water always contributes a little H₃O⁺ and OH⁻. For ordinary strong-acid concentrations (≥ about 10⁻⁵ M), that contribution is negligible compared with the acid.
Write the proton transfer as a balanced equation before you chase Ka values. Species inventory mistakes are the main source of wrong conjugate pairs.
Amphiprotic ions like HCO₃⁻ can donate or accept H⁺. Which role wins depends on Ka vs Kb for that ion compared with the partner.
sections.why: Conjugate pairs and Ka/Kb bookkeeping are the spine of every weak-acid pH problem.

worked.title: Identify conjugates for HNO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + NO₂⁻
steps: HNO₂ donates H⁺ → acid. Its conjugate base is NO₂⁻.
H₂O accepts H⁺ → base. Its conjugate acid is H₃O⁺.
Acid/base pair 1: HNO₂ / NO₂⁻. Pair 2: H₃O⁺ / H₂O.
Final answer: HNO₂ with NO₂⁻; H₃O⁺ with H₂O.

sections.heading: pH, Kw, and strong acids/bases
paragraphs: Water autoionizes: 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ with K<sub>w</sub> = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. In pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.
pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = 14.00 at 25 °C. pKa = −log Ka.
Strong acids in water (common list): HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, and H₂SO₄ for the first proton. Strong bases: group 1 hydroxides (NaOH, KOH, …) and heavy group 2 hydroxides (Ba(OH)₂, …).
For a dilute strong monoprotic acid of concentration C<sub>a</sub>, [H₃O⁺] ≈ C<sub>a</sub> and pH = −log C<sub>a</sub> (unless extremely dilute, where water's contribution matters).
For strong base C<sub>b</sub>, [OH⁻] ≈ C<sub>b</sub> (or 2 C<sub>b</sub> for Ba(OH)₂), then pOH = −log[OH⁻] and pH = 14 − pOH.
pH 7 is neutral only at 25 °C where Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. At higher T, Kw rises and neutral pH drops below 7 even though [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻].
Sig figs in pH: the digits after the decimal in pH match the sig figs in the concentration. −log(0.025) = 1.60 has two decimal places because 0.025 has two sig figs.

For Ba(OH)₂ remember the factor of two for hydroxide. For H₂SO₄ in intro courses, often treat the first proton as strong and estimate with [H₃O⁺] ≈ C for dilute solutions unless the problem asks for both steps.
pH meters report decimal values; still show the −log setup in written work so the concentration source is clear.
Scientific notation helps: −log(3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 4 − log(3.0) = 4 − 0.48 = 3.52. Practice that pattern until it is automatic.
If a strong acid concentration is 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M, you cannot ignore water; the pH is near 6.98, not 8. Ordinary course problems usually stay above 10⁻⁶ M so the simple rule works.

worked.title: pH of 0.025 M HNO₃
steps: HNO₃ is strong → [H₃O⁺] = 0.025 M.
Final answer: pH = 1.60.
Check: 10<sup>−1.60</sup> = 0.025, recovering the concentration.

workedExamples.title: pH of 0.010 M Ba(OH)₂
steps: Ba(OH)₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.020 M.
Final answer: pH = 12.30.

sections.heading: Weak acids, Ka, and salts
paragraphs: Weak acid HA: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ (or HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻) with Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA].
If Ka is small and C<sub>a</sub> is not tiny, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka C<sub>a</sub>), then pH = −log[H⁺]. Check the 5% rule: x/C<sub>a</sub> should be small.
Weak base B: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻ with Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]. Then [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb C<sub>b</sub>).
For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw. So the conjugate base of a weak acid is itself a weak base: Kb = Kw / Ka.
Salt examples: NaA (from weak HA) gives a basic solution (A⁻ hydrolyzes). NH₄Cl gives an acidic solution (NH₄⁺ is a weak acid).
Acetic acid Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ is the usual textbook value; always prefer the table your exam provides.
Percent ionization = ([H⁺]/C<sub>a</sub>) × 100%. Diluting a weak acid raises percent ionization even though pH usually rises (less acidic).
Polyprotic acids (H₂SO₄, H₂CO₃) donate protons in steps with Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂. For many intro pH estimates of H₂CO₃, Ka₁ alone is enough for a first pass.
When a salt of a weak acid and weak base dissolves, compare Ka of the cation with Kb of the anion to predict acidic vs basic.
ICE for weak acids looks like the equilibrium chapter: Initial C, 0, 0; Change −x, +x, +x; Equilibrium C−x, x, x. Then Ka = x²/(C−x).
If the approximation fails (x/C > 5%), solve the quadratic: x² + Ka x − Ka C = 0.
Salt hydrolysis: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻ with Kb = Kw/Ka. Then [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb C<sub>salt</sub>) for dilute solutions of NaA.
Buffers (next topic) deliberately mix HA and A⁻ so that pH ≈ pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). The weak-acid ICE skills here are the warm-up.
Strong vs weak is about extent of dissociation, not about concentration. A dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid; compute, do not assume.

worked.title: pH of 0.100 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵)
steps: Final answer: pH ≈ 2.87.
Optional exact check: x² + (1.8×10⁻⁵)x − (1.8×10⁻⁶) = 0.
The quadratic root is the same 1.34×10⁻³ here, confirming the approximation.

workedExamples.title: Kb of acetate if Ka(acetic) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵
steps: Final answer: Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.

workedExamples.title: Is 0.10 M NH₄Cl acidic, basic, or neutral?
steps: NH₄Cl → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻.
Cl⁻ is the conjugate of strong HCl → negligible base.
NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of weak NH₃ → weak acid.
Final answer: acidic.

mistake.wrong: Using [H⁺] = Ka for a weak acid, or treating a weak acid like a strong one with [H⁺] = C<sub>a</sub>.
mistake.whyWrong: Ka is a quotient, not the hydrogen-ion concentration. Weak acids only partially dissociate, so [H⁺] is much smaller than C<sub>a</sub>.
mistake.correct: Set up Ka = x²/(C − x), approximate if valid, then pH = −log x.

sections.heading: Structure and acid strength
paragraphs: For binary acids HX down a group (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), acid strength rises as the H–X bond weakens (HF is the weak one in water among these).
Across a period, higher electronegativity of X generally increases acidity for the same type of bond (H₂O < HF in acidity among the period-2 hydrides in the usual comparison set).
Oxoacids: more oxygen atoms or a more electronegative central atom stabilize the conjugate base and raise Ka (HClO < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄).
These trends explain table patterns; still use Ka values for numerical pH work.
Resonance in the conjugate base (as in RCOO⁻ vs RO⁻) spreads charge and increases acid strength of carboxylic acids vs alcohols.
Inductive withdrawal by electronegative substituents near the acidic H also raises Ka (Cl₃CCOOH is stronger than CH₃COOH).

Comparing acids: write the conjugate bases, ask which anion holds the negative charge more comfortably (electronegativity, size, resonance, induction). The better-stabilized anion belongs to the stronger acid.
Within oxoacids of the same central atom, each added oxygen typically raises Ka by orders of magnitude. Memorize the pattern; look up the numbers.
Binary hydrides: bond strength dominates down a group (HI > HBr > HCl ≫ HF in water). Electronegativity dominates across a short span of the table for similar structures.

worked.title: Rank acid strength: HClO₂ vs HClO₃
steps: Both are oxoacids of chlorine.
HClO₃ has more O atoms → more electron withdrawal → more stable conjugate base.
HClO₃ is the stronger acid (larger Ka).
Final answer: HClO₃ > HClO₂.
Same central atom and same charge type → oxygen count is the deciding structural clue here.
